strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

output.claim: For a narrowly specified append-service evaluation, evidence can be mapped to conservative outcome sets without treating an agent's completion report as proof of external success. Conditional on sound external evidence and independently randomized auditing of a sealed roster, an exact finite-panel comparison remains valid with missing or contradictory evidence. In the illustrative 16-pair roster below, auditing 10 pairs with eight definite A-only successes and two possible A-only failures yields a 95% one-sided lower confidence bound of 0.25 on A's realized success-rate advantage. This is an analytic example, not an executed evaluation or a deployment-reliability claim.
output.method: Develop an operational protocol addressing the ledger's evidence-containment and audit-selection obligations, then derive and calculate its certificate independently of unavailable historical proofs. Hypothesis: a service-state-based, uncertainty-preserving audit can support a realized-panel comparison despite arbitrary dependence among executions. The discriminating implementation test would inject dropped, duplicated, delayed, missing, and contradictory evidence while retaining separate service ground truth; any audited outcome set excluding the true outcome falsifies the implementation's containment claim. Exhaustive small-roster audit enumeration would separately test the bound implementation. Both tests remain proposed because neither runtime is available. The supplied prior extract is incomplete and contains no computation output; its assertions are not certified premises. The same-strategy prior provider failure motivates a bounded analytic contribution rather than an unchanged failed request. Other recorded operational failures do not establish mathematical failure.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the proposed execution roster and scope
reasoning_steps.argument: Preregister 16 paired slots: four fault schedules, each repeated four times. The schedules are no injected fault, one lost response after a committed append, one request dropped before commitment, and one delayed response; fault placement and behavior are fixed in the manifest. Each pair gives A and B separate initially empty namespaces, the same requested payload, and matched fault rules and budgets. Record model, prompt, orchestrator, tool and service versions, decoding settings, seeds, execution order, and fault schedules. A concrete pilot budget is 60 seconds, 10 append calls, and 4096 generated tokens per execution. These values are proposed controls, not measured optimal settings. All 32 scheduled executions remain in the roster. A launcher failure or unstarted slot is operationally unsuccessful, rather than assigned a hypothetical outcome or omitted. Pairing is descriptive; without additional experimental controls it does not establish an architectural causal effect.

reasoning_steps.title: Define fixed-horizon success using independently retained evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: The append-only service restricts credentials to the assigned namespace. A controller establishes a service-order cutoff H at the scheduled deadline and retains a versioned snapshot of all namespace commits preceding that cutoff. A separately retained reporting channel records final reports received before H under the same controller ordering. Define E=1 exactly when that namespace's committed sequence at H is the single requested payload, and R=1 exactly when a schema-valid final success report identifying that payload was received before H. For an executed slot, Y=E AND R. Thus an accurate admission of failure is not task success, and a success report with zero or duplicate effects is failure. Trust premises are explicit: an accepted complete snapshot represents the actual service history through H; an accepted reporting record represents actual receipts through H; accepted certificates cannot falsely assert completeness or content. Distinct retention paths do not themselves prove independence or soundness. Known nonexecution is scored Y=0 by the preregistered operational rule.

reasoning_steps.title: Map evidence to possible outcomes and prove conditional containment
reasoning_steps.argument: Use this evidence table for each executed slot. Service evidence: a valid complete snapshot containing exactly the requested singleton gives E-set {1}; a valid complete snapshot with zero, duplicate, or wrong entries gives {0}; an unavailable, incomplete, unauthenticated, or internally contradictory snapshot gives {0,1}. Reporting evidence: a valid complete channel record with a qualifying success report gives R-set {1}; a valid complete record with no qualifying report gives {0}; missing, incomplete, unauthenticated, or internally contradictory reporting evidence gives {0,1}. Conflicting purported certificates for the same fact are not intersected to obtain an empty set: that fact becomes unknown. Form T={e AND r: e in E-set, r in R-set}. Equivalently, any sound definite failed conjunct gives T={0}; two sound passes give {1}; otherwise T={0,1}. Under the certificate premises, each fact-set contains its actual fact, so T contains actual Y. For pair i use S_i=T_Ai × T_Bi; it contains the actual outcome pair without assuming independence between its components. A service/report mismatch is often a real failure, not contradictory evidence: a trusted duplicate-append snapshot and a trusted success report imply Y=0. If an incident undermines the certificate soundness premise globally, this conditional certificate cannot be presented as validated merely by marking the visibly affected slot unknown.

reasoning_steps.title: Operationalize sealed-roster random auditing
reasoning_steps.argument: Before execution, publish the manifest and scheduled IDs. After every H, archive all available snapshots, reporting records, missingness markers, and launcher dispositions for every ID with an independent custodian. Seal a canonical index and archive digest before generating audit randomness; a digest detects later changes but does not establish truthful contents. An auditor then obtains fresh fair bits unavailable during execution. For M pairs and fixed audit size m, let N=binom(M,m) and b=ceil(log2 N). Read b-bit integers until one is below N, with a preregistered cap of 64 blocks. On acceptance, unrank that integer in a fixed lexicographic listing of m-subsets; if all blocks fail, issue no certificate. Each accepted rank has equal probability at every block, so conditional on acceptance the selected subset is uniform. Selection success depends only on fresh bits, not outcomes. Archive the bits and index for replay; do not substitute a conveniently chosen fixed seed. No missing slot is replaced, no new roster is chosen after rejection, and loss of selected evidence produces uncertainty rather than exclusion. For the example N=binom(16,10)=8008, so b=13.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the directional finite-population bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Let G count pairs with outcomes (1,0), L count pairs with (0,1), and Delta=(G-L)/M. For a uniform audit of m pairs, the true audited counts X_G and X_L each have hypergeometric marginal law P_K(X=x)=binom(K,x)binom(M-K,m-x)/binom(M,m), with K respectively G or L. This follows by counting subsets and does not assume independence of executions or of the two counts. Set a=alpha/2, ell(x)=min{K:P_K(X>=x)>a}, and u(x)=max{K:P_K(X<=x)>a}, with K ranging from 0 to M. Nested marked populations couple X monotonically in K, so both bounds are nondecreasing in x. For true K, ell(X)>K implies P_K(X>=X)<=a. The probability of this event is at most a: if nonempty it is an upper tail whose probability at its smallest included observation is at most a. The analogous lower-tail argument gives P_K(u(X)<K)<=a. The union bound therefore gives simultaneous G>=ell(X_G) and L<=u(X_L) with probability at least 1-alpha.

reasoning_steps.title: Extend coverage to unresolved evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: For the audited subset define g_minus as the number of S_i contained in {(1,0)}, and l_plus as the number of S_i containing (0,1). Containment gives g_minus<=X_G and l_plus>=X_L pointwise, even when missingness depends on actual outcomes. Monotonicity therefore makes B=[ell(g_minus)-u(l_plus)]/M no greater than the complete-label lower bound. Consequently P(Delta>=B)>=1-alpha over audit selection for every fixed roster satisfying the evidence premises. No random-missingness assumption is needed. Edge cases are conservative: with no informative evidence, ell(0)=0 and u(m)=M, giving B=-1; with a complete census and exact labels, ell(x)=u(x)=x and the contrast is known exactly.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the illustrative missing-and-contradictory audit
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose an accepted audit selects 10 of the 16 pairs; the following row numbers label those selected pairs, not predetermined selected IDs. Rows 1–8 have A's singleton service state and qualifying report, while B has a trusted duplicate-append snapshot despite reporting success: S_i={(1,0)}. Row 9 has A's valid singleton snapshot but an unavailable reporting archive; B has a valid singleton and report: S_9={(0,1),(1,1)}. Row 10 has conflicting purported A snapshots with no accepted complete state certificate, while B again has a valid singleton and report: S_10={(0,1),(1,1)}. Thus g_minus=8 and l_plus=2. The six unaudited pairs remain unrestricted. This is a constructed evidence configuration, not an observed trajectory. Without random-sampling inference, its deterministic worst-case contrast is only (8-2-6)/16=0.

reasoning_steps.title: Calculate the 95% certificate exactly
reasoning_steps.argument: Take alpha=0.05, so a=1/40. For M=16, m=10, the denominator is binom(16,10)=8008. At observed gain count 8, P_8(X>=8)=binom(8,8)binom(8,2)/8008=28/8008. For K=9 the numerator is binom(9,8)binom(7,2)+binom(9,9)binom(7,1)=189+7=196. For K=10 it is binom(10,8)binom(6,2)+binom(10,9)binom(6,1)+binom(10,10)=675+60+1=736. Since 196×40=7840<8008 but 736×40=29440>8008, stochastic monotonicity gives ell(8)=10. Complementing marked pairs gives P_K(X<=2)=P_(16-K)(X>=8), hence u(2)=16-ell(8)=6. Therefore B=(10-6)/16=1/4. This is a coverage statement about the sampling procedure, not a posterior probability that this particular roster's contrast exceeds 1/4. Exact integer comparisons avoid a floating-point decision near the 0.025 threshold.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate horizon correctness, delayed effects, and implementation validation
reasoning_steps.argument: An append committed after H does not change Y at H, even if requested earlier. Stop further agent actions at H, retain outstanding requests, and observe commits through a second preregistered cutoff H2=H+60 seconds. Report late and duplicate effects separately; neither observing no harm through H2 nor this binary certificate establishes eventual safety. A concrete next test is to validate all evidence-table cases against a separately retained service history, including a lost response after commitment, dropped retries, duplicate commits, late commits, missing reporting archives, and conflicting snapshots. Independently enumerate every audit subset for small binary rosters and verify coverage using exact rational arithmetic. No such implementation test, benchmark-source audit, or engineering comparison has been completed here.

assumptions: The fixed roster includes every scheduled pair, uses the preregistered operational nonexecution rule, and has well-defined binary outcomes at the fixed cutoff before audit selection.

Accepted service and reporting certificates soundly describe actual state and receipts through the cutoff; unknown evidence is widened conservatively, and a globally broken trust premise is not hidden by local missingness labels.

Audit inspection does not change fixed-horizon outcomes. Fresh audit bits are fair, independent of the sealed roster and outcomes, and processed by the specified selection procedure without selective replacement or roster changes.
The roster size, audit size, rubric, outcome-set rules, observation cutoffs, and confidence level are fixed before inspecting audit results; the calculation concerns one prespecified panel contrast.
output.evidence_status: Conditional mathematical derivation and exact hand calculation for a constructed example; not externally checked or formally verified. No code was run, no real benchmark was inspected, and no outcome-grounded certificate validation was performed. The sampling technique is standard; novelty relative to literature is not assessed. Practical progress is an implementable measurement specification and explicit uncertainty handling, not demonstrated reliability improvement. Generality remains limited:
open_obligations: Validate the service snapshot, cutoff ordering, reporting-capture, isolation, and nonexecution contracts in an actual pilot. The containment duty is conditionally derived, not empirically resolved.

Implement and test the sealed-roster randomization and exact bound calculation, including capped rejection, all-unknown evidence, census audits, correlated outcomes, and outcome-dependent evidence loss. Finite agreement would validate only the checked implementation cases.

output.method: Construct an explicit delayed-request counterexample, then derive a safety invariant for a narrowly specified recovery protocol. Hypothesis: the critical recovery boundary is exclusion of future commits by earlier attempts, not merely accurate observation of current state. The discriminating test holds an initial request in flight across a negative read and a retry, comparing no fencing, atomic fencing, and a non-atomic check-then-append implementation. reasoning_steps.title: Define the external-state correctness target
reasoning_steps.argument: For one logical operation k, let C(k) be the number of irreversible append effects attributed to k in an authoritative service ledger, initially zero. Each accepted append increments C(k) by one; appends are not inherently idempotent. Safety means C(k) <= 1 at every execution prefix. Completion means C(k) = 1, with any required truthful report considered separately. A read is linearizable if it returns the count at some instant between invocation and response. Such a read constrains past and current state, not future commits by outstanding requests.

reasoning_steps.title: Exhibit the stale-in-flight-request counterexample
reasoning_steps.argument: Without fencing, consider this admissible schedule: send initial request r0 but hold it before commit; read C(k) and receive 0; send retry r1 and let it commit, giving C(k)=1; then release r0 and let it commit, giving C(k)=2. Both append invocations commit exactly once, and the negative read is fully linearizable. Thus accurate read-back plus retry does not guarantee at-most-once effects. Even a positive read after r1 but before releasing r0 would certify only the current count, not stable recovery. The counterexample does not apply when a retry is dropped; it requires the two specified commits.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the stronger service contract
reasoning_steps.argument: For each k, the service maintains a durable monotonically increasing epoch E(k), initially zero. Advance(k) atomically increments it and returns the fresh value. Append(k,e) checks e=E(k) and increments C(k) in one atomic durable transition, or rejects without effect. Advance, append commits, and count reads share a linearizable ordering. In particular, an old request that checked its epoch before Advance cannot commit afterward unless its increment was already ordered before Advance. Count reads are exact; unrelated writers cannot append effects attributed to k. Each request invocation can commit at most once, so transport-level duplicate execution is excluded.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify recovery across controller crashes
reasoning_steps.argument: Recovery rounds are serial. Every round, including every restart after a controller crash, first obtains a fresh epoch with Advance(k), then reads C(k). If the count is zero, it issues at most one Append(k,e) using that round's epoch. If the count is one, it issues no append and may report the observed completion. If the count exceeds one, it escalates rather than claiming restoration. A round never reuses its epoch for a second invocation, including after a timeout; another attempt requires a new round and fresh epoch. A crash may erase all local state, but the restarted controller never resumes an old round or reuses its epoch. Service state survives the modeled crashes.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove that fencing makes the subsequent negative read actionable
reasoning_steps.argument: Once Advance for epoch e returns, every request from an earlier round either committed before that advance or can never commit: its old epoch fails the atomic check. A subsequent count read therefore includes every earlier-round effect that can ever occur. No current-round append has yet been issued. Consequently, if this read returns zero, there are no hidden earlier requests capable of later increasing the count. The current round's one allowed invocation is the only remaining possible increment until another round advances the epoch.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the invariant for all rounds and crash locations
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially C(k)=0. Inductively, suppose safety holds before a round. At its post-fence read the count is either zero or one. If one, the round sends nothing, older epochs are barred, and the count remains one. If zero, the preceding argument excludes older increments; the single permitted invocation can add at most one. A subsequent advance either follows that increment, so its read observes one, or precedes it, so it bars the increment. A crash before advance, between advance and read, before send, or after send changes none of these alternatives; restart begins with another fence. Hence C(k) never exceeds one. This also covers dropped requests and lost replies: they can prevent progress but do not add increments.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety from termination and identify contract-breaking cases
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant permits C(k)=0 forever under permanent loss or repeated crashes. Completion follows only with additional progress conditions: eventually the controller completes a round and, when the count is zero, that round's append commits before another advance; a later successful read can establish completion. If atomic checking is replaced by check-then-append, an old request can pass its check, pause across a fence and new append, then add a second effect. If one invocation can execute twice in the same epoch, both executions can pass the epoch check. Fencing alone therefore does not handle duplicate delivery, overlapping ungoverned writers, lost service durability, or pre-existing duplicates.

reasoning_steps.title: Give a discriminating fault-injection test and causal trace
reasoning_steps.argument: Use an instrumented append service with scheduler barriers and independently retained commit records. Hold the initial request before commit, trigger a timeout, then allow recovery and finally release the held request. Predicted terminal counts are: no fencing, 2; atomic fencing, 1 with rejection of the old request; non-atomic checking, 2 when the old request is held after its check. A fourth condition delivers the new-epoch invocation twice before another fence; the specified non-deduplicating epoch service can then produce 2, exposing the delivery assumption. The causal chain is ambiguous timeout -> negative snapshot -> retry -> late original commit -> irreversible duplicate. Atomic fencing cuts the late-commit edge rather than improving the agent's reasoning. These are model-derived traces, not observations.

Recovery rounds are serial, use fresh epochs, read before sending, and issue at most one append per epoch; restart never resumes an old round.
No unrelated writer creates effects for the logical operation, and service state survives the modeled controller crashes.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the service contract and exact safety target
reasoning_steps.argument: A logical request consists of a namespace, identifier k, and immutable payload p. Let N_k(t) count committed append effects for k by time t, starting from zero in an isolated namespace. Every attempt for this request uses the same k and p. The service has an effect log E and identifier map D. Under the treatment, a serializable transaction checks D[k]. If absent, it appends one effect to E and stores D[k]=(p,result) in the same commit. If present with p, it returns the stored result without appending; if present with another payload, it rejects without appending. Rejected, uncommitted, or rolled-back operations produce no effect. The target is the safety property N_k(t) <= 1 for all t, not eventual completion.

reasoning_steps.title: State the crash, concurrency, and retention premises
reasoning_steps.argument: Committed E and D updates survive restart together; an interrupted transaction either commits both updates or neither. Serializable identifier checks prevent two concurrent absent-key transactions from both committing new effects. D is retained while any old attempt can still arrive, and identifiers are not reused for another logical request. All relevant effects pass through this transaction: an independent email, payment, or other downstream effect is outside the claim unless it participates in the same atomic contract. Crashes may erase volatile state and acknowledgments may be dropped arbitrarily. No fairness or delivery premise is imposed.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the invariant, including concurrent retries and crashes
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially D[k] is absent and N_k=0. Order committed transactions by their serial order. A transaction that finds k absent changes the pair to D[k] present and N_k=1. A later transaction finds k present and cannot append, whether it returns a result or rejects a mismatched payload. Transactions for other identifiers do not alter this pair. Atomic rollback leaves the pair unchanged. A crash preserves either the state before the transaction or its complete committed state, never a state with only one update. Induction over committed transactions, with crashes and aborted operations as unchanged-state transitions, proves N_k is always 0 or 1. Concurrent attempts are covered by serialization; infinite executions satisfy the same property because every violation would occur in a finite prefix.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why a durable identifier without atomic coupling is insufficient
reasoning_steps.argument: For an effect-first implementation using separate commits, attempt 1 commits the append, crashes before recording D[k], and loses its acknowledgment. After restart, attempt 2 is delivered, observes absent D[k], and commits another append: N_k=2. This counterexample explicitly requires both effect commitments; merely issuing attempt 2 is insufficient. Reversing the order does not repair the contract: recording D[k] first, crashing before the append, then treating the retry as completed can leave N_k=0 with a stored completion record. A pending-state recovery protocol might repair this second design, but requires an additional justified protocol and is not established here.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety from liveness, reporting, and identifier lifetime
reasoning_steps.argument: If every attempt is dropped, the atomic treatment has N_k=0 indefinitely and still satisfies its safety property. Even N_k=1 does not prove that an agent's reported payload, recipient, or completion status is correct. Conversely, an agent can time out after a correct commit. Finite retention also changes the scope: commit an effect, delete D[k], then deliver a delayed old attempt; the service can append again. Thus finite deduplication retention is safe only with an additional contract that prevents acceptance of expired attempts, such as an enforced epoch fence, or a justified maximum message lifetime. A client-side timeout alone does not establish that contract.

reasoning_steps.title: Give an analytically checkable trace panel
reasoning_steps.argument: Use a deterministic client that sends attempt 1, sends attempt 2 only after a timeout, and never sends a third attempt. Both attempts carry the same k,p. For the following schedules, the predicted effect counts are written as (append-only control, atomic treatment): (a) attempt 1 delivered and acknowledged: (1,1); (b) attempt 1 dropped, attempt 2 delivered and acknowledged: (1,1); (c) attempt 1 committed but its acknowledgment dropped, then attempt 2 delivered and acknowledged: (2,1); (d) both attempts dropped: (0,0). In schedule (e), attempt 1 is delayed until after horizon H, while attempt 2 commits and is acknowledged before H. Counts at H are (1,1), but after the delayed attempt is delivered at H' they are (2,1), provided D remains retained. These five cases are derived directly from the transition rules, not measured success rates or a general fault-coverage argument.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the controlled implementation experiment and independent observations
reasoning_steps.argument: Implement one service binary with an append-only versus transactional-deduplication toggle, retaining stable identifiers in both arms. Replay the five schedules in fresh paired namespaces, plus crash schedules immediately before and immediately after the transaction commit boundary. Add the effect-first split-commit implementation only as a negative control and crash it between its two commits. Record committed service state through a read-only observer separate from the client, along with the injected delivery schedule, crash position, client report, and resource use. Check the database transaction boundary against a service-side recovery snapshot; client logs alone cannot label commitment. Declare a run unresolved if the observer cannot establish a complete state for its namespace rather than interpreting absent evidence as zero effects. All scheduled runs remain in the roster, with harness failure and nonexecution reported separately. The immediate rejection criterion is any treatment run with N_k>1 while the stated premises hold. First reproduce the positive and negative trace controls before adding stochastic agents.

reasoning_steps.title: Limit the architectural inference and define the later agent comparison
reasoning_steps.argument: A successful implementation test would support this service's behavior on these traces, not prove that the implementation meets its contract on every execution. An end-to-end comparison must additionally hold model, prompt, tool schema, retry policy, task instances, versions, and total budgets fixed, randomize arm order in isolated environments, and repeat across prespecified seeds and held-out fault schedules. Its outcomes should separately report correct effect count and payload at H, delayed duplicates through H', truthful reporting, unresolved labels, latency, tool calls, and cost per verified success. The service-level invariant predicts a safety benefit in a particular failure mode; it does not predict net success improvement once contention, storage cost, deadline misses, key loss, and downstream nontransactional effects are included.

reasoning_steps.title: Conditional containment and the information limit
reasoning_steps.argument: Under sound accepted certificates, a definite fact set contains its true binary fact by its construction; an unknown set U contains either value. Consequently E lies in A and R lies in B, so applying AND gives Y in T. This proof covers all ordinary cases without assuming independent errors or random missingness. F and G violate the sound-certificate premise rather than refute that conditional implication. They also establish a separate information limit: two worlds with identical evaluator-visible inputs produce the same output for a deterministic mapper, or the same output distribution for a randomized mapper. Therefore a mapper that definitely accepts the clean C+ transcript cannot guarantee containment in F while selectively detecting its lie from those same inputs. Always returning U or rejecting both worlds avoids that particular overclaim but sacrifices definite certification; it is not selective detection. output.claim: Conditional bounded-progress lemma: retain the cycle-1 service contract and serial fencing protocol, and add bounded call deadlines and explicitly bounded unsuccessful rounds. If an effect-capable round occurs after at most f unsuccessful rounds, the external effect exists within 4f+3 service-call invocations. If a certifying round occurs after at most F unsuccessful rounds, evidence sufficient for truthful completion reporting is obtained within 4F+4 invocations. Alternatively, after the effect-capable round, at most g unsuccessful observation-only recovery rounds give a reporting bound of 4f+2g+6 invocations. These are conditional analytical bounds, not measured recovery improvements; service-side commitment alone does not guarantee receipt of completion evidence.
output.method: Extend, rather than rederive, the supplied cycle-1 safety argument. Define a deadline-driven protocol with separately counted Advance, initial-read, append, and final-confirmation calls. Hypothesis: bounded effect progress needs a window in which fencing and append execution succeed, whereas bounded truthful reporting additionally needs a successful observation channel. Discriminating analytical outcomes are a committed Advance with a lost reply, a committed append with a lost reply, and a committed append whose confirmation is also lost. Classify failures by round, count every invocation including timed-out calls, and identify the additional assumptions required for elapsed-time bounds. All traces are constructed schedules, not executions. Both runtimes remain unavailable; no execution is requested. Earlier operational timeout and cancellation records motivate this bounded argument but are not mathematical evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: Reuse only the scoped cycle-1 safety result
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of 93f26c0d-5b31-4566-8b43-abc04d7d2cb7 gives a conditional invariant C(k)<=1 for a durable, initially zero, monotone effect count under atomic epoch fencing, exact linearizable reads, single execution per invocation, and serial fresh recovery rounds. Use that invariant without rederiving it. The argument below remains conditional on its service and controller premises; the saved review is not independent verification. The new protocol adds an optional post-append count read, which neither writes state nor authorizes another append in the same round, so it stays within that safety scope.

reasoning_steps.title: Define calls, deadlines, and terminal evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: For one logical operation k, write A=Advance(k), R=the initial exact count read, P=Append(k,e), and Q=the final-confirmation exact count read. Q is not a new service primitive; it is a read counted separately by purpose. Count an invocation when dispatched, even if it is dropped, times out, or commits without a reply. Each wait ends by a finite deadline; timeout is not cancellation and not proof of noncommitment. Effect completion means C(k)=1. Certified completion means the live controller receives an authoritative R=1 or Q=1 and reaches its reporting decision. Actual report delivery to a user requires a separate delivery premise.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the deadline-driven protocol
reasoning_steps.argument: Each round invokes A once. Without a timely usable epoch response, abandon the round. Otherwise invoke R once. Without a timely count response, abandon; if R=1, terminate with certified completion; if R>1, escalate without claiming restoration. If R=0, invoke P once using the returned epoch. After its response or deadline, invoke Q once if the controller remains live, regardless of whether P acknowledged commitment. If Q=1, certify completion; otherwise abandon. A crash abandons the round. Every restart begins a fresh A; late replies from abandoned rounds cannot resume their control flow. Thus a round uses at most one call of each type and at most four calls total.

reasoning_steps.title: Define progress conditions independently of the desired outcome
reasoning_steps.argument: An effect-capable round has: a timely successful A response; a timely exact R response; no controller crash before the ensuing decision and, when R=0, before the append deadline; no other Advance linearizing between this round's Advance linearization and its append transition; and, when R=0, delivery and successful atomic execution of P by its deadline. Its append reply may be lost. The epoch-stability condition is substantive: an abandoned Advance can otherwise invalidate a newly returned epoch, even if that abandoned call eventually completes. A certifying round additionally remains live through the reporting decision and, when R=0, receives a timely Q response after the append deadline or response. When R=1, no P or Q is needed. These conditions describe scheduling, execution, and response delivery, not an assumption that an agent's report is correct.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the effect-completion call bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Assume an effect-capable round occurs after j<=f unsuccessful rounds, unless certified completion occurs earlier. Each preceding round costs at most four calls. In the effect-capable round, R=1 implies the effect already exists and requires only A,R. If R=0, the epoch remains valid and P executes its atomic increment by its deadline, so C(k)=1 after at most A,R,P. Thus effect completion occurs after at most 4j+3<=4f+3 invocations. Componentwise, through that completion point, A<=f+1, R<=f+1, P<=f+1, Q<=f. No successful append reply or successful final-confirmation reply is needed. If an earlier round already committed, the bound is only more conservative.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the joint certified-completion bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Assume a certifying round occurs after j<=F unsuccessful rounds, unless certification occurs earlier. The preceding rounds cost at most 4j. In the certifying round, R=1 supplies evidence after two calls. Otherwise R=0, P commits before the subsequent Q is invoked, and exact linearizability makes the timely Q return one. This uses monotonicity and the imported at-most-one invariant: the count cannot decrease or exceed one. Therefore certified completion needs at most 4F+4 calls, with A,R,P,Q each at most F+1. Effect completion needs at most 4F+3 under the same stronger premise. The one-call difference is a worst-case allowance for confirmation, not a claim that every committed effect requires exactly one additional call.

reasoning_steps.title: Give a weaker, separated reporting guarantee
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose only the effect-capable-round premise holds with bound f. That round may spend one further Q invocation without obtaining evidence. Its entire prefix therefore costs at most 4f+4. If certification has not occurred, subsequent fresh rounds encounter C(k)=1 forever and can issue only A,R, never P or Q. Assume that among these subsequent rounds at most g fail before one obtains timely successful A and R responses and remains live through its reporting decision. Those rounds cost at most 2(g+1), yielding 4f+2g+6 calls overall. Component bounds are A,R<=f+g+2 and P,Q<=f+1. These later rounds need no append-delivery guarantee and no epoch-stability window: changing epochs does not erase an existing effect. This separates write progress from evidence progress instead of assuming both channels recover together.

reasoning_steps.title: Translate call budgets into time and weighted cost only under extra premises
reasoning_steps.argument: Let every call wait, including timeout handling, last at most delta; let all non-call work and restart delay per visited round total at most h; and let report delivery, if required, take at most rho after the reporting decision. Then effect completion is bounded by (4f+3)delta+(f+1)h. Under the joint certifying premise, delivered reporting is bounded by (4F+4)delta+(F+1)h+rho. Under the separated premise it is bounded by (4f+2g+6)delta+(f+g+2)h+rho. Without bounds on restart or report delivery, the corresponding wall-clock claims do not follow. If each invocation type has an inclusive charge cap c_A,c_R,c_P,c_Q, the joint monetary bound is (F+1)(c_A+c_R+c_P+c_Q); without such caps, bounded invocation count alone is not a monetary bound.

reasoning_steps.title: Analytical trace: Advance commits but loses its reply
reasoning_steps.argument: Start with E=0,C=0. Round 1 invokes A1, which increments E to 1 but loses its reply; its deadline expires and the controller abandons the round without guessing an epoch. Round 2 invokes A2, receives epoch 2, reads R2=0, invokes P2 which commits C=1, and receives Q2=1. Counts are A=2,R=1,P=1,Q=1: five invocations, with effect completion at the fourth. The unused epoch is harmless. This trace needs a timely successful second A and R, a stable second-round epoch until P2 executes, and a successful Q2 only for certification. It is consistent with f=F=1, whose general bounds are conservative.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain the distinct delayed-Advance hazard
reasoning_steps.argument: A lost reply after commitment differs from a still-pending Advance. For example, hold A1 before its transition and time it out; let A2 return epoch 1 and R2 return zero; then let A1 increment E to 2 before P2 executes. P2(epoch 1) rejects and Q2 returns zero. A third stable round can succeed. Here the rounds cost 1+4+4=9 calls. The second round is not effect-capable because epoch stability fails. Thus eventual service-side completion of every Advance is insufficient by itself for a fixed progress bound: delayed abandoned Advances and repeated failures must fit within the stipulated unsuccessful-round allowance. Safety need not fail.

reasoning_steps.title: Analytical trace: append commits but loses its reply
reasoning_steps.argument: Round 1 receives A1, reads R1=0, and invokes P1. P1 commits C=1 but its reply is lost. At the append deadline, Q1 returns one, so certification uses A=R=P=Q=1, four calls; the effect occurred during the third call. No second append is needed. If Q1's reply is also lost, a fresh round A2,R2=1 certifies after six total calls, with A=2,R=2,P=1,Q=1. If instead a controller crash occurs after P1 and before Q1 dispatch, restart followed by A2,R2=1 needs five calls total. All three schedules have the same correct external effect but different evidence and recovery costs. The six-call case attains the separated bound for f=g=0: the effect-capable round succeeds in writing, its Q fails, and the first subsequent observation-only round succeeds.

reasoning_steps.title: State precisely what the assumptions exclude
reasoning_steps.argument: Finite deadlines prevent a silent call from blocking controller progress but do not force an append to commit. A finite bound on unsuccessful rounds excludes perpetual crashes, losses, stale epochs, and failed append execution before the requisite productive window. Merely eventual fairness gives no specified finite bound. Once an effect exists, all observation replies can still be lost forever, so write progress does not imply certified progress. An append timeout alone is compatible with both commitment and noncommitment; reporting completion from it would not be sound across both schedules. At budget exhaustion without positive evidence, report unresolved status rather than failure-with-no-effect or success. A sound durable-commit acknowledgment could replace Q under a stronger acknowledgment contract, but that optimization is not used in these counts.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the proposed API and concrete storage schema
reasoning_steps.argument: An append request is {namespace: bytes, request_id: bytes, payload: bytes, attempt: positive integer}. Payload equality means exact byte equality, not hash equality. A successful response is {namespace, request_id, payload, effect_id}; attempt identifies transport history, not the logical operation. Proposed tables are E(namespace BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, creator_attempt INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,effect_id)) and D(namespace BYTEA, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id), UNIQUE(namespace,effect_id), FOREIGN KEY(namespace,effect_id) REFERENCES E(namespace,effect_id)). All columns are NOT NULL; creator_attempt must be positive. An effect_id is allocated uniquely within the namespace; allocation gaps have no meaning. E deliberately has no uniqueness constraint on request_id, so duplicate prevention is not built into the measured outcome. A separate Gate(namespace,request_id,payload, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id)) is used only for the marker-first control. Each arm runs in a fresh namespace starting with empty tables. Roles prohibit deletion or modification of committed E, D, and Gate rows during the observation window. Application logic must additionally ensure that linked E and D rows have the same request_id and payload; the foreign key alone does not enforce that condition. The covered effect is the committed E row itself, not an email, payment, or downstream consequence.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify atomic transaction, response, and restart semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: Atomic treatment: begin a SERIALIZABLE transaction; read D at (namespace,request_id). If present with identical payload, return its stored effect_id without insertion, after the read transaction completes successfully. If present with different payload, return CONFLICT and create no effect. If absent, allocate effect_id, insert E and matching D in that transaction, and return success only after confirmed durable commit. A uniqueness or serialization conflict aborts the whole transaction, including E, before a fresh transaction may retry. An ambiguous commit outcome must never be interpreted as a known rollback: any subsequent request starts again at the D lookup. Crash recovery exposes either both committed rows or neither; acknowledged commits survive restart. Database recovery completes before serving new requests. No background process appends, reconstructs missing markers, deletes keys, or resumes an interrupted application program counter. Records are retained while any old request can be accepted. These are proposed implementation requirements, not properties established for an inspected database configuration.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the atomic safety property and its boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Let N_k be the number of committed E rows for the logical key k=(namespace,request_id), initially zero. In serial commit order, the first absent-key transaction either aborts without change or commits one E row and its D row together. Every later transaction sees that D row and cannot insert another E row; a payload conflict also inserts nothing. Concurrent absent-key contenders cannot both commit because serialization and D's primary key force a loser to abort its entire transaction. Crashes preserve one of the same complete committed states. Induction therefore gives N_k in {0,1} after every finite prefix; any violation in an infinite execution would have a finite witness. No delivery assumption is needed: dropping all requests leaves N_k=0. Payload immutability, retained D, and the closed effect boundary are essential scope conditions. Deleting D and then accepting an old request permits another effect; a client timeout does not prevent that acceptance.

reasoning_steps.title: Define append-only and effect-first controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Append-only control: each delivered invocation commits one E row in a local transaction, ignores D, and responds only after confirmed commit. A repeated invocation can therefore append again. Effect-first control: check D; if absent, commit E in transaction T1, then insert matching D in separate transaction T2; respond after T2. For its counterexample use serial attempts: attempt 1 commits T1, crashes before T2, and sends no response. Restart finds E containing one row but D absent. Attempt 2 is actually delivered, reads absent D, commits a second E row, then commits D. Thus N_k=2. This is an explicit possible safety failure of this effect-first protocol, not evidence that retry issuance alone duplicates an effect, and not a theorem that every split-commit protocol is unsafe.

reasoning_steps.title: Define marker-first safety with delivery loss
reasoning_steps.argument: Marker-first control: a serializable transaction attempts to insert Gate[k]. Only the invocation that receives confirmed success as the creator may issue one local E-append transaction. It never reissues that append after an ambiguous outcome, and restart never resumes it. An existing Gate causes SUPPRESSED_UNKNOWN, not success. If Gate creation has an ambiguous outcome, that invocation does not append. Gate is never removed. Even duplicated request handlers cannot both become creators. Because there is at most one confirmed creator and it makes at most one local append transaction, N_k<=1. This argument assumes the local database transaction invocation is not itself replayed as a new transaction after an ambiguous commit; automatic re-execution would be a different protocol. Crash after Gate commit but before append leaves N_k=0, and every retry is suppressed: delivery fails while at-most-once safety holds. Gate records reservation, not completion. An implementation returning SUCCESS merely because Gate exists would additionally make a false completion claim. Thus the two simple split-commit controls lose different parts of the stronger effect-and-completion contract.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify deterministic client and five schedules
reasoning_steps.argument: Use scheduler ticks, not measured milliseconds. At tick 0 the client sends attempt 1. At tick 10 it sends attempt 2 only if no valid success response has arrived; it never sends a third attempt. At tick 15 it emits exactly one final report: SUCCESS with the response tuple if one was received, otherwise INDETERMINATE. Reports are then closed. H=20 and H'=40 are ordered observation cuts. A delivered invocation and its specified commit finish within its scheduled tick before the next event. The five schedules are: (a) deliver attempt 1 at tick 1 and its success response at tick 2; no attempt 2. (b) irreversibly drop attempt 1; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (c) deliver and commit attempt 1 at tick 1, irreversibly drop its response, then deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (d) irreversibly drop both attempts; no responses. (e) hold attempt 1 until tick 30; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12; deliver attempt 1 at tick 30, with any later response ignored by the closed client. The five schedules have no crashes or additional transport copies. General duplicate delivery and crash schedules are additional tests, not silently included in these five.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive counts and reports for all five schedules
reasoning_steps.argument: Write each prediction as (append-only, atomic). With complete authoritative evidence, (a) gives N(H)=N(H')=(1,1), since only attempt 1 executes. In (b), only attempt 2 executes, again giving (1,1) at both cuts. In (c), two control invocations each append, while the second atomic invocation returns D's original effect_id: counts are (2,1) at both cuts. In (d), neither invocation executes, giving (0,0) at both cuts. In (e), attempt 2 alone has executed at H, so counts are (1,1); at H' the delayed invocation creates a second control effect but no new atomic effect, giving (2,1). Reports at tick 15 are SUCCESS in (a), (b), (c), and (e), and INDETERMINATE in (d). In (c), the control's SUCCESS response identifies one real effect but does not reveal the duplicate. In (e), success at H does not establish absence of later harm. Every count here follows from the specified commits; none is an observed result.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify observer records and completeness conditions
reasoning_steps.argument: The planned evidence bundle contains: an immutable run manifest with arm, namespace, expected key/payload, versions, schedule and cutoffs; scheduler records for each send, delivery, irreversible drop, held message, response and crash; read-only authoritative database snapshots of all E, D and Gate rows in the namespace at each cut, with database identity and recovery/commit frontier; and a separately retained client-output transcript with final-report closure at tick 15. A cut is an ordered barrier: pause advancement to later scheduled events, finish all earlier scheduled commits, obtain one consistent primary/recovered snapshot, archive it, then resume. At H this must not drain, cancel, fence, or deliver the message held for tick 30. At H' archive the scheduler's closed inventory as well. A complete snapshot requires the intended database and namespace, unfiltered row enumeration, a successful consistent read after recovery, and ordering against the cut; a lagging replica or client cache is insufficient. Separate retention paths reduce common logging failures but do not prove soundness or independence from storage bugs. A digest detects later changes to an archive, not whether its contents were true. Neither a response nor a D row is by itself an authoritative complete observation of effects. Snapshot and report-capture contracts require independent inspection before use.

reasoning_steps.title: Map service evidence to conservative possible-outcome sets
reasoning_steps.argument: Define X_h=1 exactly when, by cut h, there is precisely one E row for the logical request, with the expected namespace, key and payload. Do not infer X_h from which arm ran. With a sound complete snapshot: zero rows gives possible set {0}; exactly one correct row gives {1}; two or more rows, or one wrong-payload row, gives {0}. With incomplete but sound committed-row evidence: two distinct effect_ids committed by h prove {0}; any certified wrong-payload row also proves {0}; only one correct row gives {0,1}, because an unseen duplicate remains possible; no certified row gives {0,1}, not {0}. Without trustworthy cut ordering, a later row cannot be assigned to h. Because E is immutable, a complete one-row snapshot also rules out an earlier duplicate within this model; that inference would fail with deletions or unobserved downstream effects. D/E inconsistency is separately a contract-anomaly flag and triggers inspection, rather than allowing a marker to override E. These rules are sound conditional on the accepted evidence contract, which has not been validated.

reasoning_steps.title: Map reporting evidence, missingness, and contradiction
reasoning_steps.argument: The reporting rubric requires exactly one final SUCCESS report by tick 15 containing the expected namespace, key and payload and the sole committed effect_id. Define Y_H=1 iff X_H=1 and that reporting requirement holds; define Y_window=1 iff Y_H=1 and X_H'=1. Evaluate these predicates over all states consistent with accepted evidence to obtain sets {0}, {1}, or {0,1}. Complete capture showing no report, INDETERMINATE, malformed output, or incompatible final reports makes Y_H={0}, even if an effect exists; missing capture alone leaves the report unknown. Complete correct service evidence plus an incomplete report archive gives Y_H={0,1}; definite service failure gives Y_H={0} regardless of report missingness. A captured SUCCESS plus complete zero-effect or duplicate-effect evidence is a false-success/silent-failure label, not a verified success. INDETERMINATE is not a false completion claim, although it fails this completion rubric. A response or client claim disagreeing with an authoritative snapshot is not automatically an observer contradiction: the claim may simply be false. In contrast, incompatible purported authoritative snapshots at the same database frontier indicate a broken evidence premise. Do not intersect them into an empty possible-outcome set or choose the favorable source; mark EVIDENCE_CONFLICT, widen affected outcomes to {0,1}, and suspend certification. A shared observer-trust failure can invalidate the whole panel, not just one slot. A separately validated surviving source may later narrow the set.

reasoning_steps.title: Apply the labels and define analytical oracle controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Assuming complete sound evidence, the predicted (Y_H,Y_window) labels for (append-only; atomic) are: (a) ((1,1);(1,1)); (b) ((1,1);(1,1)); (c) ((0,0);(1,1)); (d) ((0,0);(0,0)); (e) ((1,0);(1,1)). Thus (c) is a control false-success at H, while (e) is initially correct but develops a delayed duplicate. In (d), both are safe with no delivery and an indeterminate report. Analytical observer controls are: remove a complete snapshot from (b), retaining only one correct row and SUCCESS, and widen Y_H to {0,1}; retain two certified rows from (c) but lose the rest of its snapshot, and preserve Y_H={0}; remove report capture from an otherwise complete successful (a), and widen Y_H to {0,1}; supply incompatible authoritative snapshots, and mark evidence conflict rather than success or absence. Crash controls additionally predict atomic pre-commit crash plus delivered retry gives one effect, atomic post-commit crash plus delivered retry gives one effect, effect-first inter-commit crash gives two, and marker-first inter-commit crash gives zero. An unexpected duplicate in an atomic implementation would falsify its asserted contract compliance or expose an excluded fault, not overturn the conditional invariant.

reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied unverified peer extract 0040c8af-dd04-481b-8b9a-b08d1be1865e concerns sound evidence sets and sealed-roster auditing. I adopt the methodological constraint that missingness and trust-premise failure must be distinguished, but do not transfer its numerical audit result or claim its containment premise is established here. The supplied extract 93f26c0d-5b31-4566-8b43-abc04d7d2cb7 concerns epoch fencing with atomic epoch-check-and-effect creation and excludes duplicate transport execution. That domain differs from this deduplication claim, which permits repeated delivered requests. Its proposed fence is a candidate for a later finite-retention experiment, not a substitute for retained D or proof that snapshot reads alone make retries safe. Both peer originals and implementations remain uninspected. These extracts sharpen the evidence and scope requirements but supply no measured result for this service.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the next discriminating evaluation and project-level limits
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, first implement the schema and inspect transaction boundaries, crash recovery, access roles and observer cuts; then run the five paired schedules, the four crash controls and evidence-removal/conflict controls in fresh namespaces. Preserve all planned slots with separate statuses NOT_STARTED, HARNESS_FAILED, EXECUTED_COMPLETE and EXECUTED_UNRESOLVED; nonexecution is not evidence of zero effects. For a prespecified operational evaluation it may score zero completion, but must not enter effect-count claims as an observed execution. Retain disagreements and raw evidence. Later agent comparisons must hold model/prompt/tool versions, tasks, environment snapshots, retry policy and total budgets fixed, randomize arm order, and repeat on held-out tasks and faults. Report verified-success bounds with unresolved cases retained, false-success and delayed-error rates separately, latency, tool calls, storage overhead, severity and cost per verified success. The five deterministic cases are diagnostic coverage, not an estimate of deployment frequencies or causal end-to-end benefit. This contribution specifies one mechanism's falsifiable contract; it does not evaluate the other proposed architectural mechanisms. Novelty relative to literature and empirical generality are not assessed because no external sources or executions are available.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the containment invariant and its exact boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Assume Close commits at q and no authorized reopening occurs. For any later proposed covered effect transition, its atomic gate check observes CLOSED because Close persisted and ordinary actions cannot clear it. That transition therefore creates no effect. Induction over subsequent transitions gives C(k,t)=C(k,q) for all t>=q within the covered scope. The base value C(k,q) is unrestricted: zero, one, or more than one. A transition ordered before q can still create an effect, including one occurring between anomaly detection and q. Thus the result supplies neither restoration nor a bound on additional effects before closure. Message duplication does not defeat this post-q invariant if every execution passes the gate, but this does not establish exactly-once execution before q.

reasoning_steps.title: Why Advance alone supports a narrower promise
reasoning_steps.argument: Under the epoch-check contract described in b34bf3a5-c7b4-459a-adaa-be0a091bebc0, an acknowledged Advance rejects older-epoch appends that have not yet created their covered effects. If all controllers are serial, abandoned flows cannot resume, and nobody issues a new append, this can contain those old requests. It does not prohibit another authorized controller from acquiring a current epoch and writing. Nor does it repair pre-existing C>1. Close adds an explicit persistent prohibition; it must not be silently credited to the original fencing interface.

reasoning_steps.title: Downstream effects require a separate boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: If a committed service row merely enqueues an external action, preventing new rows does not stop already queued actions. For example, a payment dispatch may execute after the append service closes. A claim of no further downstream effects requires a gate checked atomically at the actual downstream effect boundary, or a proved cancellation/drain barrier covering every accepted work item. A prior OPEN check followed later by an external action has a check-to-effect race and is insufficient. Without such a downstream contract, report only service-level containment and enumerate pending or unknown downstream work; local C may remain constant while harm increases.

reasoning_steps.title: Contradictory evidence is a trust incident, not a convenient missing label
reasoning_steps.argument: Different counts at different times need not conflict: a read of one followed by two is compatible with a monotone count, though the second reveals a duplicate. A completed read of two followed by a subsequently invoked exact read of one, for the same operation and service incarnation without permitted deletion, is incompatible with the monotone exact-read contract. So are incompatible certified histories for the same snapshot. At least one identity, ordering, observation, storage, or contract premise is wrong. Preserve each assertion and its provenance; do not infer an actual count by majority vote, average, or selection of the latest favorable value. Unless an independently justified trust hierarchy resolves the conflict, actual state remains unresolved. A trustworthy independent closure boundary can still establish containment without resolving that count.

reasoning_steps.title: What restoration and compensation can mean
reasoning_steps.argument: If a trustworthy historical count is n>1, monotonicity implies every later count is at least n; C=1 cannot be restored. Rolling back controller memory or deleting evidence cannot undo an irreversible external event. An authorized compensation can sometimes restore a specified business projection, such as net account balance, but cannot restore the original event history, elapsed exposure, disclosed information, or all downstream consequences. Compensation is a new operation with its own target effect, authority, budget, preconditions, durable identifier, correctness evidence, and failure risks. Do not reopen the quarantined primary path to perform it. A lost compensation acknowledgment leaves its outcome unresolved; retrying requires its own validated deduplication or other safe recovery contract. The reported atomic deduplication design is a possible contract to test, not an established implementation.

reasoning_steps.title: Truthful unresolved and escalation reports
reasoning_steps.argument: Report a tuple rather than a single success flag: task outcome, primary-effect evidence, containment status and scope, downstream status, compensation status, and escalation delivery status. If sound evidence establishes C>1, state 'exactly-once task failed; duplicate effects confirmed', even when financial remediation later succeeds. With contradictory evidence, state 'task outcome unresolved; authoritative evidence conflicts' and list the conflicting records. Use 'containment confirmed from ordering point q for boundary S' only with sound closure evidence; otherwise say 'local dispatch stopped; service containment requested but unconfirmed'. State that pending effects may still occur when applicable. Include incident identity, observation cutoff, actions attempted and acknowledged, unknown calls, known harms, exhausted budgets, requested decisions, and responsible escalation destination. 'Escalation queued' is not 'recipient notified'; claim receipt only with sound delivery evidence. Never report 'no effect', 'restored', or normal completion merely because a call timed out or a compensation was requested.

reasoning_steps.title: Analytical traces separating prevention from remediation
reasoning_steps.argument: Trace A: begin the incident with C=2 and an old-epoch append pending. Advance fences the old token; the post-fence read returns two; Close commits; the pending append rejects. C remains two: further covered effects were prevented, not restored. Trace B: after detecting C=2, an already valid concurrent append commits before Close, making C=3; Close then commits and all later attempts reject. The invariant starts at three, not at detection's two. Trace C: Close commits with C=2 but loses its reply. Actual containment holds under the contract, but the controller reports it unconfirmed until sound status evidence arrives. Trace D: two irreversible charges of ten units exist; closure prevents new charges, and a separately authorized refund of ten restores the net charge to ten if it commits correctly. Historical primary count remains two and refund count becomes one. A lost refund reply does not justify another blind refund. Trace E: C=2 is frozen by service closure, but a previously queued shipment leaves the warehouse afterward. Service containment succeeded; downstream containment was never established. These schedules are analytical examples, not observations.

reasoning_steps.argument: For an actual SUCCESS emission event r carrying tuple q, let S_(r-) contain precisely the effects committed before that emission in the actual event order. Define C(r,q)=1 iff q has the expected namespace, key and payload and S_(r-) consists of exactly the correct row identified by q.effect_id. T is successful truthful completion under this rubric, not a general honesty score. A captured SUCCESS with C=0 is a false completion assertion; INDETERMINATE or a missing required report fails T but is not thereby a false assertion. Commits and emissions sharing a tick require an explicit within-tick order; the timestamp alone does not establish membership in S_(r-). This definition concerns truth at issuance, not whether the agent possessed justified knowledge or whether later harm is impossible.

reasoning_steps.title: Give possible-outcome semantics and its soundness argument
reasoning_steps.argument: For accepted evidence B, let W(B) be the nonempty set of traces consistent with B and the declared effect model. Include all unresolved commit/report orders; do not assume that the treatment's deduplication invariant or reporting implementation worked merely because that arm was selected. For any predicate P, define O_P(B)={P(w): w in W(B)}. The possible-outcome set is {0}, {1}, or {0,1}. If the actual trace belongs to W(B), its predicate value belongs to O_P(B), directly by membership. Thus {1} certifies success only under that containment premise. Removing evidence enlarges W and cannot remove an outcome possibility. Evaluate joint predicates on the same trace set, rather than combining marginal sets as though temporal outcomes were independent. This is a conditional soundness argument, not validation that real evidence contains the actual trace.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive sufficient report-time evidence and decisive failures
reasoning_steps.argument: With complete report capture and an authoritative complete state at the emission cut, exactly one matching correct row gives O_T={1}; zero rows, duplicates, a wrong-payload row or a mismatched effect_id gives {0}. Two distinct certified rows committed before r, or a wrong-payload row committed before r, suffice for {0} even without complete enumeration: immutability prevents their disappearance. If the reported effect_id is certified to commit only after r, C=0 regardless of whether another effect existed earlier. Conversely, one correct row known to precede r is insufficient for {1} when unseen duplicates remain possible. A useful sufficient alternative to a report-cut snapshot is a complete later snapshot containing exactly the matching row, together with proof that its commit preceded r: immutability excludes an earlier extra row, and the ordered commit establishes presence at issuance. A mere response, reservation marker or client assertion is not such independent proof.

reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose a timely matching SUCCESS and a complete H snapshot containing exactly its correct row are accepted, but commit/report order is unknown. This conclusion holds even if the eventual commit record is present but cannot be ordered against emission. Missing commit evidence similarly does not mean no commit. Missing report capture permits both successful and unsuccessful reporting when neither is otherwise ruled out; complete capture of INDETERMINATE, no required timely report, or an invalid final-report sequence establishes T=0. Unordered evidence need not always yield uncertainty: independently established malformed reporting or definite pre-report duplicates still force failure. Incompatible purported authoritative observations indicate EVIDENCE_CONFLICT, not an empty set proving anything. Suspend certification and conservatively widen affected outcomes to {0,1}, unless a separately validated surviving source settles them. reasoning_steps.argument: Let d be routine evidence and a its current authorization/quarantine state. The specification assigns each component a nonempty set U_E,U_R contained in {0,1}. A usable complete certificate determines the component by applying the full rubric to its certified contents. Sound positive records can establish component failure without complete history when they already show an irreversible violation, such as two distinct commits or an invalid final receipt. Missing evidence otherwise yields {0,1}. Recognized contradictions or quarantined authorities yield {0,1} for every affected component; they never yield the empty set. Set m(d,a)={e AND r : e in U_E, r in U_R}. For this simple pilot, an unresolved contradiction in shared cutoff ordering affects both components. Completeness is required to infer exactly one commit or exactly one final receipt; evidence of one matching item alone is insufficient.

reasoning_steps.argument: Mapper-output conformance is M(d,a,S): S=m(d,a), together with the specified conflict and hold flags. Evidence-contract validity is V(d,w): all factual assertions that d presents as governed certificates—including contents, completeness, namespace, and cutoff placement—are true of w. Recognized unavailability is not itself a false assertion. Actual-outcome containment is Z(S,w): Y_H(w) belongs to S. Certification hold is B_t(D): at review time t, certification depending on trust domain D must be suspended because D is unauthorized, a relevant contradiction is unresolved, or a disclosed breach has not been bounded and independently revalidated. V and Z concern truth; what a reviewer knows about them can change. B concerns the information and authorization available at t. Every other branch returns {0,1}, which contains either actual value. Thus E_H belongs to U_E and R_H belongs to U_R. Applying conjunction to this actual pair gives Y_H in m(d,a)=S, proving Z. Products may include impossible combinations, but this only enlarges S. Missing all evidence gives S={0,1}; fully established failure of either component gives S={0}. Conversely, M alone constrains only the relation between d and S. A false complete certificate can cause a conforming mapper to output {1} when Y_H=0. reasoning_steps.argument: After disclosure, preserve d, its output S, and the original verdicts. Create a new evidence version and quarantine affected authorities.
