reasoning_steps.title: Define the proposed API and concrete storage schema
reasoning_steps.argument: An append request is {namespace: bytes, request_id: bytes, payload: bytes, attempt: positive integer}. Payload equality means exact byte equality, not hash equality. A successful response is {namespace, request_id, payload, effect_id}; attempt identifies transport history, not the logical operation. Proposed tables are E(namespace BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, creator_attempt INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,effect_id)) and D(namespace BYTEA, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id), UNIQUE(namespace,effect_id), FOREIGN KEY(namespace,effect_id) REFERENCES E(namespace,effect_id)). All columns are NOT NULL; creator_attempt must be positive. An effect_id is allocated uniquely within the namespace; allocation gaps have no meaning. E deliberately has no uniqueness constraint on request_id, so duplicate prevention is not built into the measured outcome. A separate Gate(namespace,request_id,payload, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id)) is used only for the marker-first control. Each arm runs in a fresh namespace starting with empty tables. Roles prohibit deletion or modification of committed E, D, and Gate rows during the observation window. Application logic must additionally ensure that linked E and D rows have the same request_id and payload; the foreign key alone does not enforce that condition. The covered effect is the committed E row itself, not an email, payment, or downstream consequence.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify atomic transaction, response, and restart semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: Atomic treatment: begin a SERIALIZABLE transaction; read D at (namespace,request_id). If present with identical payload, return its stored effect_id without insertion, after the read transaction completes successfully. If present with different payload, return CONFLICT and create no effect. If absent, allocate effect_id, insert E and matching D in that transaction, and return success only after confirmed durable commit. A uniqueness or serialization conflict aborts the whole transaction, including E, before a fresh transaction may retry. An ambiguous commit outcome must never be interpreted as a known rollback: any subsequent request starts again at the D lookup. Crash recovery exposes either both committed rows or neither; acknowledged commits survive restart. Database recovery completes before serving new requests. No background process appends, reconstructs missing markers, deletes keys, or resumes an interrupted application program counter. Records are retained while any old request can be accepted. These are proposed implementation requirements, not properties established for an inspected database configuration.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the atomic safety property and its boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Let N_k be the number of committed E rows for the logical key k=(namespace,request_id), initially zero. In serial commit order, the first absent-key transaction either aborts without change or commits one E row and its D row together. Every later transaction sees that D row and cannot insert another E row; a payload conflict also inserts nothing. Concurrent absent-key contenders cannot both commit because serialization and D's primary key force a loser to abort its entire transaction. Crashes preserve one of the same complete committed states. Induction therefore gives N_k in {0,1} after every finite prefix; any violation in an infinite execution would have a finite witness. No delivery assumption is needed: dropping all requests leaves N_k=0. Payload immutability, retained D, and the closed effect boundary are essential scope conditions. Deleting D and then accepting an old request permits another effect; a client timeout does not prevent that acceptance.

reasoning_steps.title: Define append-only and effect-first controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Append-only control: each delivered invocation commits one E row in a local transaction, ignores D, and responds only after confirmed commit. A repeated invocation can therefore append again. Effect-first control: check D; if absent, commit E in transaction T1, then insert matching D in separate transaction T2; respond after T2. For its counterexample use serial attempts: attempt 1 commits T1, crashes before T2, and sends no response. Restart finds E containing one row but D absent. Attempt 2 is actually delivered, reads absent D, commits a second E row, then commits D. Thus N_k=2. This is an explicit possible safety failure of this effect-first protocol, not evidence that retry issuance alone duplicates an effect, and not a theorem that every split-commit protocol is unsafe.

reasoning_steps.title: Define marker-first safety with delivery loss
reasoning_steps.argument: Marker-first control: a serializable transaction attempts to insert Gate[k]. Only the invocation that receives confirmed success as the creator may issue one local E-append transaction. It never reissues that append after an ambiguous outcome, and restart never resumes it. An existing Gate causes SUPPRESSED_UNKNOWN, not success. If Gate creation has an ambiguous outcome, that invocation does not append. Gate is never removed. Even duplicated request handlers cannot both become creators. Because there is at most one confirmed creator and it makes at most one local append transaction, N_k<=1. This argument assumes the local database transaction invocation is not itself replayed as a new transaction after an ambiguous commit; automatic re-execution would be a different protocol. Crash after Gate commit but before append leaves N_k=0, and every retry is suppressed: delivery fails while at-most-once safety holds. Gate records reservation, not completion. An implementation returning SUCCESS merely because Gate exists would additionally make a false completion claim. Thus the two simple split-commit controls lose different parts of the stronger effect-and-completion contract.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify deterministic client and five schedules
reasoning_steps.argument: Use scheduler ticks, not measured milliseconds. At tick 0 the client sends attempt 1. At tick 10 it sends attempt 2 only if no valid success response has arrived; it never sends a third attempt. At tick 15 it emits exactly one final report: SUCCESS with the response tuple if one was received, otherwise INDETERMINATE. Reports are then closed. H=20 and H'=40 are ordered observation cuts. A delivered invocation and its specified commit finish within its scheduled tick before the next event. The five schedules are: (a) deliver attempt 1 at tick 1 and its success response at tick 2; no attempt 2. (b) irreversibly drop attempt 1; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (c) deliver and commit attempt 1 at tick 1, irreversibly drop its response, then deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (d) irreversibly drop both attempts; no responses. (e) hold attempt 1 until tick 30; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12; deliver attempt 1 at tick 30, with any later response ignored by the closed client. The five schedules have no crashes or additional transport copies. General duplicate delivery and crash schedules are additional tests, not silently included in these five.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive counts and reports for all five schedules
reasoning_steps.argument: Write each prediction as (append-only, atomic). With complete authoritative evidence, (a) gives N(H)=N(H')=(1,1), since only attempt 1 executes. In (b), only attempt 2 executes, again giving (1,1) at both cuts. In (c), two control invocations each append, while the second atomic invocation returns D's original effect_id: counts are (2,1) at both cuts. In (d), neither invocation executes, giving (0,0) at both cuts. In (e), attempt 2 alone has executed at H, so counts are (1,1); at H' the delayed invocation creates a second control effect but no new atomic effect, giving (2,1). Reports at tick 15 are SUCCESS in (a), (b), (c), and (e), and INDETERMINATE in (d). In (c), the control's SUCCESS response identifies one real effect but does not reveal the duplicate. In (e), success at H does not establish absence of later harm. Every count here follows from the specified commits; none is an observed result.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify observer records and completeness conditions
reasoning_steps.argument: The planned evidence bundle contains: an immutable run manifest with arm, namespace, expected key/payload, versions, schedule and cutoffs; scheduler records for each send, delivery, irreversible drop, held message, response and crash; read-only authoritative database snapshots of all E, D and Gate rows in the namespace at each cut, with database identity and recovery/commit frontier; and a separately retained client-output transcript with final-report closure at tick 15. A cut is an ordered barrier: pause advancement to later scheduled events, finish all earlier scheduled commits, obtain one consistent primary/recovered snapshot, archive it, then resume. At H this must not drain, cancel, fence, or deliver the message held for tick 30. At H' archive the scheduler's closed inventory as well. A complete snapshot requires the intended database and namespace, unfiltered row enumeration, a successful consistent read after recovery, and ordering against the cut; a lagging replica or client cache is insufficient. Separate retention paths reduce common logging failures but do not prove soundness or independence from storage bugs. A digest detects later changes to an archive, not whether its contents were true. Neither a response nor a D row is by itself an authoritative complete observation of effects. Snapshot and report-capture contracts require independent inspection before use.

reasoning_steps.title: Map service evidence to conservative possible-outcome sets
reasoning_steps.argument: Define X_h=1 exactly when, by cut h, there is precisely one E row for the logical request, with the expected namespace, key and payload. Do not infer X_h from which arm ran. With a sound complete snapshot: zero rows gives possible set {0}; exactly one correct row gives {1}; two or more rows, or one wrong-payload row, gives {0}. With incomplete but sound committed-row evidence: two distinct effect_ids committed by h prove {0}; any certified wrong-payload row also proves {0}; only one correct row gives {0,1}, because an unseen duplicate remains possible; no certified row gives {0,1}, not {0}. Without trustworthy cut ordering, a later row cannot be assigned to h. Because E is immutable, a complete one-row snapshot also rules out an earlier duplicate within this model; that inference would fail with deletions or unobserved downstream effects. D/E inconsistency is separately a contract-anomaly flag and triggers inspection, rather than allowing a marker to override E. These rules are sound conditional on the accepted evidence contract, which has not been validated.

reasoning_steps.title: Map reporting evidence, missingness, and contradiction
reasoning_steps.argument: The reporting rubric requires exactly one final SUCCESS report by tick 15 containing the expected namespace, key and payload and the sole committed effect_id. Define Y_H=1 iff X_H=1 and that reporting requirement holds; define Y_window=1 iff Y_H=1 and X_H'=1. Evaluate these predicates over all states consistent with accepted evidence to obtain sets {0}, {1}, or {0,1}. Complete capture showing no report, INDETERMINATE, malformed output, or incompatible final reports makes Y_H={0}, even if an effect exists; missing capture alone leaves the report unknown. Complete correct service evidence plus an incomplete report archive gives Y_H={0,1}; definite service failure gives Y_H={0} regardless of report missingness. A captured SUCCESS plus complete zero-effect or duplicate-effect evidence is a false-success/silent-failure label, not a verified success. INDETERMINATE is not a false completion claim, although it fails this completion rubric. A response or client claim disagreeing with an authoritative snapshot is not automatically an observer contradiction: the claim may simply be false. In contrast, incompatible purported authoritative snapshots at the same database frontier indicate a broken evidence premise. Do not intersect them into an empty possible-outcome set or choose the favorable source; mark EVIDENCE_CONFLICT, widen affected outcomes to {0,1}, and suspend certification. reasoning_steps.title: Define the proposed API and concrete storage schema
reasoning_steps.argument: An append request is {namespace: bytes, request_id: bytes, payload: bytes, attempt: positive integer}. Payload equality means exact byte equality, not hash equality. A successful response is {namespace, request_id, payload, effect_id}; attempt identifies transport history, not the logical operation. Proposed tables are E(namespace BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, creator_attempt INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,effect_id)) and D(namespace BYTEA, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id), UNIQUE(namespace,effect_id), FOREIGN KEY(namespace,effect_id) REFERENCES E(namespace,effect_id)). All columns are NOT NULL; creator_attempt must be positive. An effect_id is allocated uniquely within the namespace; allocation gaps have no meaning. E deliberately has no uniqueness constraint on request_id, so duplicate prevention is not built into the measured outcome. A separate Gate(namespace,request_id,payload, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id)) is used only for the marker-first control. Each arm runs in a fresh namespace starting with empty tables. Roles prohibit deletion or modification of committed E, D, and Gate rows during the observation window. Application logic must additionally ensure that linked E and D rows have the same request_id and payload; the foreign key alone does not enforce that condition. The covered effect is the committed E row itself, not an email, payment, or downstream consequence.

review.rationale: These are proposed premises, not inspected implementation facts. The E schema permits duplicate request identifiers, D supplies logical-key uniqueness, and the text explicitly identifies linked-row consistency as an additional application obligation rather than falsely attributing it to the foreign key.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify atomic transaction, response, and restart semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: Atomic treatment: begin a SERIALIZABLE transaction; read D at (namespace,request_id). If present with identical payload, return its stored effect_id without insertion, after the read transaction completes successfully. If present with different payload, return CONFLICT and create no effect. If absent, allocate effect_id, insert E and matching D in that transaction, and return success only after confirmed durable commit. A uniqueness or serialization conflict aborts the whole transaction, including E, before a fresh transaction may retry. An ambiguous commit outcome must never be interpreted as a known rollback: any subsequent request starts again at the D lookup. Crash recovery exposes either both committed rows or neither; acknowledged commits survive restart. Database recovery completes before serving new requests. No background process appends, reconstructs missing markers, deletes keys, or resumes an interrupted application program counter. Records are retained while any old request can be accepted. These are proposed implementation requirements, not properties established for an inspected database configuration.

review.rationale: Under the conditional claim, atomic rollback includes E, ambiguous commits are resolved through a new D lookup, and restart never blindly resumes an old append. These requirements close the specified duplicate-creation paths without asserting an actual database satisfies them.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the atomic safety property and its boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Let N_k be the number of committed E rows for the logical key k=(namespace,request_id), initially zero. In serial commit order, the first absent-key transaction either aborts without change or commits one E row and its D row together. Every later transaction sees that D row and cannot insert another E row; a payload conflict also inserts nothing. Concurrent absent-key contenders cannot both commit because serialization and D's primary key force a loser to abort its entire transaction. Crashes preserve one of the same complete committed states. Induction therefore gives N_k in {0,1} after every finite prefix; any violation in an infinite execution would have a finite witness. No delivery assumption is needed: dropping all requests leaves N_k=0. Payload immutability, retained D, and the closed effect boundary are essential scope conditions. Deleting D and then accepting an old request permits another effect; a client timeout does not prevent that acceptance.

review.rationale: The first successful absent-key transaction creates both rows. D's unique key forces competing transactions to abort their E writes, and retained D prevents later insertion. Complete-state crash recovery preserves the invariant; a safety violation in an infinite execution would have a finite witness. The proof can use serialization order rather than identifying it with physical commit order.

reasoning_steps.title: Define append-only and effect-first controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Append-only control: each delivered invocation commits one E row in a local transaction, ignores D, and responds only after confirmed commit. A repeated invocation can therefore append again. Effect-first control: check D; if absent, commit E in transaction T1, then insert matching D in separate transaction T2; respond after T2. For its counterexample use serial attempts: attempt 1 commits T1, crashes before T2, and sends no response. Restart finds E containing one row but D absent. Attempt 2 is actually delivered, reads absent D, commits a second E row, then commits D. Thus N_k=2. This is an explicit possible safety failure of this effect-first protocol, not evidence that retry issuance alone duplicates an effect, and not a theorem that every split-commit protocol is unsafe.

review.rationale: The specified effect-first trace explicitly commits both effects, with the first crash leaving D absent. It therefore establishes an existential safety failure of that protocol without assuming that merely issuing a retry creates another effect.

reasoning_steps.title: Define marker-first safety with delivery loss
reasoning_steps.argument: Marker-first control: a serializable transaction attempts to insert Gate[k]. Only the invocation that receives confirmed success as the creator may issue one local E-append transaction. It never reissues that append after an ambiguous outcome, and restart never resumes it. An existing Gate causes SUPPRESSED_UNKNOWN, not success. If Gate creation has an ambiguous outcome, that invocation does not append. Gate is never removed. Even duplicated request handlers cannot both become creators. Because there is at most one confirmed creator and it makes at most one local append transaction, N_k<=1. This argument assumes the local database transaction invocation is not itself replayed as a new transaction after an ambiguous commit; automatic re-execution would be a different protocol. Crash after Gate commit but before append leaves N_k=0, and every retry is suppressed: delivery fails while at-most-once safety holds. Gate records reservation, not completion. An implementation returning SUCCESS merely because Gate exists would additionally make a false completion claim. Thus the two simple split-commit controls lose different parts of the stronger effect-and-completion contract.

review.rationale: Persistent Gate uniqueness permits at most one confirmed creator, and the explicitly restricted creator issues at most one non-replayed append transaction. A crash between reservation and append then leaves zero effects with permanent suppression. This establishes the claimed safety/delivery distinction within that restricted protocol.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify deterministic client and five schedules
reasoning_steps.argument: Use scheduler ticks, not measured milliseconds. At tick 0 the client sends attempt 1. At tick 10 it sends attempt 2 only if no valid success response has arrived; it never sends a third attempt. At tick 15 it emits exactly one final report: SUCCESS with the response tuple if one was received, otherwise INDETERMINATE. Reports are then closed. H=20 and H'=40 are ordered observation cuts. A delivered invocation and its specified commit finish within its scheduled tick before the next event. The five schedules are: (a) deliver attempt 1 at tick 1 and its success response at tick 2; no attempt 2. (b) irreversibly drop attempt 1; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (c) deliver and commit attempt 1 at tick 1, irreversibly drop its response, then deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (d) irreversibly drop both attempts; no responses. (e) hold attempt 1 until tick 30; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12; deliver attempt 1 at tick 30, with any later response ignored by the closed client. The five schedules have no crashes or additional transport copies. General duplicate delivery and crash schedules are additional tests, not silently included in these five.

review.rationale: These are explicit analytical schedule premises. Response timing determines whether attempt 2 exists, held delivery remains pending across H, and the no-extra-fault condition makes the panel reproducible as a specification rather than an empirical estimate.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive counts and reports for all five schedules
reasoning_steps.argument: Write each prediction as (append-only, atomic). With complete authoritative evidence, (a) gives N(H)=N(H')=(1,1), since only attempt 1 executes. In (b), only attempt 2 executes, again giving (1,1) at both cuts. In (c), two control invocations each append, while the second atomic invocation returns D's original effect_id: counts are (2,1) at both cuts. In (d), neither invocation executes, giving (0,0) at both cuts. In (e), attempt 2 alone has executed at H, so counts are (1,1); at H' the delayed invocation creates a second control effect but no new atomic effect, giving (2,1). Reports at tick 15 are SUCCESS in (a), (b), (c), and (e), and INDETERMINATE in (d). In (c), the control's SUCCESS response identifies one real effect but does not reveal the duplicate. In (e), success at H does not establish absence of later harm. Every count here follows from the specified commits; none is an observed result.

review.rationale: Schedules a and b execute one invocation, c executes two before both cuts, d executes none, and e executes one before H and two before H'. Append-only execution counts every invocation; atomic execution suppresses the repeated logical request. The stipulated responses also entail the stated tick-15 reports.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify observer records and completeness conditions
reasoning_steps.argument: The planned evidence bundle contains: an immutable run manifest with arm, namespace, expected key/payload, versions, schedule and cutoffs; scheduler records for each send, delivery, irreversible drop, held message, response and crash; read-only authoritative database snapshots of all E, D and Gate rows in the namespace at each cut, with database identity and recovery/commit frontier; and a separately retained client-output transcript with final-report closure at tick 15. A cut is an ordered barrier: pause advancement to later scheduled events, finish all earlier scheduled commits, obtain one consistent primary/recovered snapshot, archive it, then resume. At H this must not drain, cancel, fence, or deliver the message held for tick 30. At H' archive the scheduler's closed inventory as well. A complete snapshot requires the intended database and namespace, unfiltered row enumeration, a successful consistent read after recovery, and ordering against the cut; a lagging replica or client cache is insufficient. Separate retention paths reduce common logging failures but do not prove soundness or independence from storage bugs. A digest detects later changes to an archive, not whether its contents were true. Neither a response nor a D row is by itself an authoritative complete observation of effects. Snapshot and report-capture contracts require independent inspection before use.

review.rationale: The proposed barrier and complete-snapshot requirements distinguish authoritative state from client logs and avoid consuming the held message at H. The step correctly treats authenticity, completeness, and ordering as premises requiring validation; archive digests alone are not offered as proof of truth.

reasoning_steps.title: Map service evidence to conservative possible-outcome sets
reasoning_steps.argument: Define X_h=1 exactly when, by cut h, there is precisely one E row for the logical request, with the expected namespace, key and payload. Do not infer X_h from which arm ran. With a sound complete snapshot: zero rows gives possible set {0}; exactly one correct row gives {1}; two or more rows, or one wrong-payload row, gives {0}. With incomplete but sound committed-row evidence: two distinct effect_ids committed by h prove {0}; any certified wrong-payload row also proves {0}; only one correct row gives {0,1}, because an unseen duplicate remains possible; no certified row gives {0,1}, not {0}. Without trustworthy cut ordering, a later row cannot be assigned to h. Because E is immutable, a complete one-row snapshot also rules out an earlier duplicate within this model; that inference would fail with deletions or unobserved downstream effects. D/E inconsistency is separately a contract-anomaly flag and triggers inspection, rather than allowing a marker to override E. These rules are sound conditional on the accepted evidence contract, which has not been validated.

review.rationale: For the defined fixed-cut predicate, complete enumeration determines the count, while two certified distinct effects or a wrong-payload effect suffice to prove failure despite incomplete enumeration. A lone correct effect cannot rule out an unseen duplicate. These implications depend on trustworthy cutoff ordering and immutable covered effects, as stated.

reasoning_steps.title: Map reporting evidence, missingness, and contradiction
reasoning_steps.argument: The reporting rubric requires exactly one final SUCCESS report by tick 15 containing the expected namespace, key and payload and the sole committed effect_id. Define Y_H=1 iff X_H=1 and that reporting requirement holds; define Y_window=1 iff Y_H=1 and X_H'=1. Evaluate these predicates over all states consistent with accepted evidence to obtain sets {0}, {1}, or {0,1}. Complete capture showing no report, INDETERMINATE, malformed output, or incompatible final reports makes Y_H={0}, even if an effect exists; missing capture alone leaves the report unknown. Complete correct service evidence plus an incomplete report archive gives Y_H={0,1}; definite service failure gives Y_H={0} regardless of report missingness. A captured SUCCESS plus complete zero-effect or duplicate-effect evidence is a false-success/silent-failure label, not a verified success. INDETERMINATE is not a false completion claim, although it fails this completion rubric. A response or client claim disagreeing with an authoritative snapshot is not automatically an observer contradiction: the claim may simply be false. In contrast, incompatible purported authoritative snapshots at the same database frontier indicate a broken evidence premise. Do not intersect them into an empty possible-outcome set or choose the favorable source; mark EVIDENCE_CONFLICT, widen affected outcomes to {0,1}, and suspend certification. A shared observer-trust failure can invalidate the whole panel, not just one slot. A separately validated surviving source may later narrow the set.

review.rationale: The possible-set and evidence-conflict rules are conservative for the stated fixed-horizon predicates, and a false client claim need not imply conflicting observers. However, service correctness at H does not establish that a completion report was true when issued.
review.objection: Y_H can equal 1 when SUCCESS is emitted at tick 15 before any effect exists and the effect commits at tick 18. Add a report-time state predicate, or explicitly label Y_H as horizon correctness plus timely reporting rather than truthful completion at report time.

reasoning_steps.title: Apply the labels and define analytical oracle controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Assuming complete sound evidence, the predicted (Y_H,Y_window) labels for (append-only; atomic) are: (a) ((1,1);(1,1)); (b) ((1,1);(1,1)); (c) ((0,0);(1,1)); (d) ((0,0);(0,0)); (e) ((1,0);(1,1)). Thus (c) is a control false-success at H, while (e) is initially correct but develops a delayed duplicate. In (d), both are safe with no delivery and an indeterminate report. Analytical observer controls are: remove a complete snapshot from (b), retaining only one correct row and SUCCESS, and widen Y_H to {0,1}; retain two certified rows from (c) but lose the rest of its snapshot, and preserve Y_H={0}; remove report capture from an otherwise complete successful (a), and widen Y_H to {0,1}; supply incompatible authoritative snapshots, and mark evidence conflict rather than success or absence. Crash controls additionally predict atomic pre-commit crash plus delivered retry gives one effect, atomic post-commit crash plus delivered retry gives one effect, effect-first inter-commit crash gives two, and marker-first inter-commit crash gives zero. An unexpected duplicate in an atomic implementation would falsify its asserted contract compliance or expose an excluded fault, not overturn the conditional invariant.

review.rationale: For the five prescribed schedules, successful effects precede reporting, so the displayed Y_H and Y_window pairs follow from the counts and report tuples. The missing-evidence controls widen uncertainty without turning absence into zero, while two certified duplicates still establish failure. These checks do not cover the late-commit reporting gap.

reasoning_steps.title: Assess peer relevance without transferring unsupported results
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied unverified peer extract 0040c8af-dd04-481b-8b9a-b08d1be1865e concerns sound evidence sets and sealed-roster auditing. I adopt the methodological constraint that missingness and trust-premise failure must be distinguished, but do not transfer its numerical audit result or claim its containment premise is established here. The supplied extract 93f26c0d-5b31-4566-8b43-abc04d7d2cb7 concerns epoch fencing with atomic epoch-check-and-effect creation and excludes duplicate transport execution. That domain differs from this deduplication claim, which permits repeated delivered requests. Its proposed fence is a candidate for a later finite-retention experiment, not a substitute for retained D or proof that snapshot reads alone make retries safe. Both peer originals and implementations remain uninspected. These extracts sharpen the evidence and scope requirements but supply no measured result for this service.

review.rationale: The measurement peer's sound-evidence premise complements the observer proposal without validating it. The recovery peer assumes atomic fencing and excludes duplicate transport execution, unlike this branch's repeated-delivery model. The step correctly declines to transfer its safety result as a replacement for deduplication.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the next discriminating evaluation and project-level limits
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, first implement the schema and inspect transaction boundaries, crash recovery, access roles and observer cuts; then run the five paired schedules, the four crash controls and evidence-removal/conflict controls in fresh namespaces. Preserve all planned slots with separate statuses NOT_STARTED, HARNESS_FAILED, EXECUTED_COMPLETE and EXECUTED_UNRESOLVED; nonexecution is not evidence of zero effects. For a prespecified operational evaluation it may score zero completion, but must not enter effect-count claims as an observed execution. Retain disagreements and raw evidence. Later agent comparisons must hold model/prompt/tool versions, tasks, environment snapshots, retry policy and total budgets fixed, randomize arm order, and repeat on held-out tasks and faults. The five deterministic cases are diagnostic coverage, not an estimate of deployment frequencies or causal end-to-end benefit. This contribution specifies one mechanism's falsifiable contract; it does not evaluate the other proposed architectural mechanisms. Novelty relative to literature and empirical generality are not assessed because no external sources or executions are available.

review.rationale: This is a proposed evaluation sequence, not a measured result. Preserving planned slots, separating nonexecution from observed effect counts, retaining raw evidence, and controlling versions and budgets address real comparison hazards. The step appropriately withholds deployment-frequency, causal-benefit, and novelty claims.

objective_review.claim: Conditional on: Each logical request starts in a fresh namespace with zero effects; accepted attempts preserve its request identifier and exact payload; The atomic arm uses serializable transactions whose E and D writes commit or roll back together, with durable committed state surviving modeled crashes; All covered effects are immutable E rows created through the specified service; no unmodeled downstream effect, corruption, deletion, or bypass writer is included; Deduplication records remain retained throughout acceptance of old attempts, and identifiers are not reused for different operations; Evidence-to-label soundness is conditional on authentic, complete where claimed, correctly ordered authoritative snapshots and final-report capture; contradictory authoritative evidence suspends that premise; The five analytical schedule predictions assume the exact deliveries, drops, response timings, and commit completions specified in the schedule, with no additional faults. Conditional on the Investigator's listed storage, request-lifetime, effect-boundary, evidence, and schedule assumptions, atomic append-and-deduplication guarantees at most one covered committed effect per logical request. The proposed contracts support the five analytical effect-count and fixed-horizon completion predictions, but do not establish report-time truth, implementation compliance, or measured reliability improvement.
objective_review.argument_summary: A successful absent-key transaction creates one immutable effect and its retained deduplication record atomically. The record's unique key and whole-transaction rollback prevent concurrent losers or subsequent requests from adding another effect. Crashes preserve complete committed states. The explicit effect-first trace creates two effects; the marker-first trace reserves the key and loses delivery without duplication. The five schedules follow directly from their prescribed deliveries and commits. Conservative evidence sets correctly avoid treating missing observations as zero effects. Their fixed-horizon reporting predicate nevertheless needs an additional temporal distinction to support a claim of truthful completion when the report was issued.

argument_steps.title: Define the proposed API and concrete storage schema
argument_steps.argument: An append request is {namespace: bytes, request_id: bytes, payload: bytes, attempt: positive integer}. Payload equality means exact byte equality, not hash equality. A successful response is {namespace, request_id, payload, effect_id}; attempt identifies transport history, not the logical operation. Proposed tables are E(namespace BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, creator_attempt INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,effect_id)) and D(namespace BYTEA, request_id BYTEA, payload BYTEA, effect_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id), UNIQUE(namespace,effect_id), FOREIGN KEY(namespace,effect_id) REFERENCES E(namespace,effect_id)). All columns are NOT NULL; creator_attempt must be positive. An effect_id is allocated uniquely within the namespace; allocation gaps have no meaning. E deliberately has no uniqueness constraint on request_id, so duplicate prevention is not built into the measured outcome. A separate Gate(namespace,request_id,payload, PRIMARY KEY(namespace,request_id)) is used only for the marker-first control. Each arm runs in a fresh namespace starting with empty tables. Roles prohibit deletion or modification of committed E, D, and Gate rows during the observation window. Application logic must additionally ensure that linked E and D rows have the same request_id and payload; the foreign key alone does not enforce that condition. The covered effect is the committed E row itself, not an email, payment, or downstream consequence.

review.rationale: These are proposed premises, not inspected implementation facts. The E schema permits duplicate request identifiers, D supplies logical-key uniqueness, and the text explicitly identifies linked-row consistency as an additional application obligation rather than falsely attributing it to the foreign key.

argument_steps.title: Specify atomic transaction, response, and restart semantics
argument_steps.argument: Atomic treatment: begin a SERIALIZABLE transaction; read D at (namespace,request_id). If present with identical payload, return its stored effect_id without insertion, after the read transaction completes successfully. If present with different payload, return CONFLICT and create no effect. If absent, allocate effect_id, insert E and matching D in that transaction, and return success only after confirmed durable commit. A uniqueness or serialization conflict aborts the whole transaction, including E, before a fresh transaction may retry. An ambiguous commit outcome must never be interpreted as a known rollback: any subsequent request starts again at the D lookup. Crash recovery exposes either both committed rows or neither; acknowledged commits survive restart. Database recovery completes before serving new requests. No background process appends, reconstructs missing markers, deletes keys, or resumes an interrupted application program counter. Records are retained while any old request can be accepted. These are proposed implementation requirements, not properties established for an inspected database configuration.

review.rationale: Under the conditional claim, atomic rollback includes E, ambiguous commits are resolved through a new D lookup, and restart never blindly resumes an old append. These requirements close the specified duplicate-creation paths without asserting an actual database satisfies them.

argument_steps.title: Derive the atomic safety property and its boundaries
argument_steps.argument: Let N_k be the number of committed E rows for the logical key k=(namespace,request_id), initially zero. In serial commit order, the first absent-key transaction either aborts without change or commits one E row and its D row together. Every later transaction sees that D row and cannot insert another E row; a payload conflict also inserts nothing. Concurrent absent-key contenders cannot both commit because serialization and D's primary key force a loser to abort its entire transaction. Crashes preserve one of the same complete committed states. Induction therefore gives N_k in {0,1} after every finite prefix; any violation in an infinite execution would have a finite witness. No delivery assumption is needed: dropping all requests leaves N_k=0. Payload immutability, retained D, and the closed effect boundary are essential scope conditions. Deleting D and then accepting an old request permits another effect; a client timeout does not prevent that acceptance.

review.rationale: The first successful absent-key transaction creates both rows. D's unique key forces competing transactions to abort their E writes, and retained D prevents later insertion. Complete-state crash recovery preserves the invariant; a safety violation in an infinite execution would have a finite witness. The proof can use serialization order rather than identifying it with physical commit order.

argument_steps.title: Define append-only and effect-first controls
argument_steps.argument: Append-only control: each delivered invocation commits one E row in a local transaction, ignores D, and responds only after confirmed commit. A repeated invocation can therefore append again. Effect-first control: check D; if absent, commit E in transaction T1, then insert matching D in separate transaction T2; respond after T2. For its counterexample use serial attempts: attempt 1 commits T1, crashes before T2, and sends no response. Restart finds E containing one row but D absent. Attempt 2 is actually delivered, reads absent D, commits a second E row, then commits D. Thus N_k=2. This is an explicit possible safety failure of this effect-first protocol, not evidence that retry issuance alone duplicates an effect, and not a theorem that every split-commit protocol is unsafe.

review.rationale: The specified effect-first trace explicitly commits both effects, with the first crash leaving D absent. It therefore establishes an existential safety failure of that protocol without assuming that merely issuing a retry creates another effect.

argument_steps.title: Define marker-first safety with delivery loss
argument_steps.argument: Marker-first control: a serializable transaction attempts to insert Gate[k]. Only the invocation that receives confirmed success as the creator may issue one local E-append transaction. It never reissues that append after an ambiguous outcome, and restart never resumes it. An existing Gate causes SUPPRESSED_UNKNOWN, not success. If Gate creation has an ambiguous outcome, that invocation does not append. Gate is never removed. Even duplicated request handlers cannot both become creators. Because there is at most one confirmed creator and it makes at most one local append transaction, N_k<=1. This argument assumes the local database transaction invocation is not itself replayed as a new transaction after an ambiguous commit; automatic re-execution would be a different protocol. Crash after Gate commit but before append leaves N_k=0, and every retry is suppressed: delivery fails while at-most-once safety holds. Gate records reservation, not completion. An implementation returning SUCCESS merely because Gate exists would additionally make a false completion claim. Thus the two simple split-commit controls lose different parts of the stronger effect-and-completion contract.

review.rationale: Persistent Gate uniqueness permits at most one confirmed creator, and the explicitly restricted creator issues at most one non-replayed append transaction. A crash between reservation and append then leaves zero effects with permanent suppression. This establishes the claimed safety/delivery distinction within that restricted protocol.

argument_steps.title: Specify deterministic client and five schedules
argument_steps.argument: Use scheduler ticks, not measured milliseconds. At tick 0 the client sends attempt 1. At tick 10 it sends attempt 2 only if no valid success response has arrived; it never sends a third attempt. At tick 15 it emits exactly one final report: SUCCESS with the response tuple if one was received, otherwise INDETERMINATE. Reports are then closed. H=20 and H'=40 are ordered observation cuts. A delivered invocation and its specified commit finish within its scheduled tick before the next event. The five schedules are: (a) deliver attempt 1 at tick 1 and its success response at tick 2; no attempt 2. (b) irreversibly drop attempt 1; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (c) deliver and commit attempt 1 at tick 1, irreversibly drop its response, then deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12. (d) irreversibly drop both attempts; no responses. (e) hold attempt 1 until tick 30; deliver attempt 2 at tick 11 and its response at tick 12; deliver attempt 1 at tick 30, with any later response ignored by the closed client. The five schedules have no crashes or additional transport copies. General duplicate delivery and crash schedules are additional tests, not silently included in these five.

review.rationale: These are explicit analytical schedule premises. Response timing determines whether attempt 2 exists, held delivery remains pending across H, and the no-extra-fault condition makes the panel reproducible as a specification rather than an empirical estimate.

artifacts.claim_or_question: Conditional on the stated ordering, isolation, and evidence-soundness premises, the proposed evidence mapper contains actual fixed-horizon E, R, and Y. The finite conformance specification below distinguishes execution failure, recognized evidence uncertainty, and a broken trust premise. In particular, a silently false completeness certificate can exclude the actual outcome without any inconsistency visible to the routine evaluator: an evaluator accepting an identical truthful transcript cannot selectively detect that substitution without additional evidence. The suite is specified but unexecuted; it does not establish operational soundness or improved agent reliability.
artifacts.method: Specify a minimal append-service/controller contract and 17 deterministic cases, including positive and negative controls. Hypothesis: an implementation obeying the contract preserves outcome containment despite lost responses, dropped retries, duplicates, late effects, and recognized evidence loss. Discriminating outcomes are an incorrect evidence set, exclusion of independently established actual E/R/Y, retrospective alteration of the H label, or failure to suspend certification after a demonstrated trust breach. The reference observer is held out from the routine mapper until comparison; otherwise the test would merely check agreement with evidence already used to score the run. Each case starts from a fresh empty namespace with fixed payload p. Fault schedules, implementation versions, event ordering, evidence presented, and expected outputs must be frozen before execution. These are conformance tests, not stochastic success-rate estimates or architectural causal comparisons. Neither runtime is available, so no program or execution is claimed. The recorded same-strategy provider failure motivates this bounded specification rather than repeating a failed request.

artifacts.skeptic_response:
Cycle 2 supplies a useful analytical specification: 17 cases distinguish external effects, reporting receipts, delayed effects, missing evidence, visible contradictions, and silent certificate failures. The conditional containment argument is valid under the listed soundness premises. All cases remain unexecuted; neither runtime is available, and no implementation or real-service evidence was supplied.

One material correction is needed. Step 4 classifies any exclusion of actual E/R/Y as mapper nonconformance. In F and G, however, the specified mapper returns exactly its prescribed evidence-based output; false certificates cause the exclusion. These cases demonstrate failure of the evidence contract and end-to-end containment, not necessarily incorrect implementation of the mapper. Separate those verdicts explicitly.

The remaining central applicability gap is reference validity. An independently retained record is useful only if its placement and capture actually cover every relevant durable commit or ingress receipt. The proposed reference witnesses are requirements, not validated observers. A concrete capture and cutoff protocol, with crash-boundary falsification controls, would advance this duty without requiring an unavailable execution.

The fixed-H rubric also intentionally permits a success report before the effect exists, provided the effect commits before H. It therefore measures eventual-by-H effect plus receipt, not truthful reporting at receipt time. This is a scope limitation rather than a refutation of the stated lemma.

reasoning_steps.title: Continuity and the unresolved duty
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of 0040c8af-dd04-481b-8b9a-b08d1be1865e defines E as singleton external state, R as receipt of a qualifying success report, and Y=E AND R. Its containment argument explicitly assumes sound certificates; it does not validate them. This submission addresses the unresolved evidence-containment and service-contract duties, particularly bf3247b81dbbb0694a4ca71eb191de2a2126c25df87ccae3ef9d857e06a753fc and d88fb2d3015c70ec8d8d486e86e1472892f06e50837f8bc3e7e32a36410f7b3d. The ledger marks audit-selection specification addressed, not its implementation validated. The truncated f59b1252-c29e-4f4a-a888-f436ab9a93aa supplies the recorded dropped-retry restriction: sending a retry does not imply another commit. That restriction is implemented directly in cases D+ and D− below. Missing originals, 15 omitted findings, and 49 omitted historical obligations remain unassessed.

reasoning_steps.title: Minimal service and controller contract
reasoning_steps.argument: Each executed case has one initially empty namespace and immutable requested payload p. An append commit atomically adds an immutable entry with a unique commit ID; entries cannot be erased. Distinct commits of p count separately, including commits caused by retries or duplicate delivery. No idempotency or eventual-delivery guarantee is assumed. Requests, admissions, commits, responses, and report receipts are distinct events. A response is not the effect. Credentials isolate the namespace, and every covered effect must appear in its authoritative state. The controller defines one total ordering of actual commits, report receipts, and cutoff markers. A real implementation must enforce this ordering at commit/receipt boundaries or supply an equivalent consistent-cut protocol; timestamps on ordinary logs alone are insufficient. Use scheduled H=60 seconds and H2=120 seconds, with marker precedence deciding events at the same wall-clock time. An event precedes H exactly when it is ordered before its marker. At H, stop new agent submissions; previously admitted requests may still commit. Observation continues without changing the H outcome.

reasoning_steps.title: Outcome definitions and evidence objects
reasoning_steps.argument: Let L_H be the ordered sequence of all namespace payloads committed before H. E=1 iff L_H=[p]. R=1 iff at least one schema-valid success report naming the run, namespace, and p was actually received by the reporting ingress before H. A false claim of external success can still make R=1; E tests its external consequence. For executed slots Y=E AND R. Reports received after H do not count. An authenticated service certificate C_S names the run, namespace, H marker, history version, ordered commit IDs/payloads, and claimed completeness through H. A reporting certificate C_R similarly names H and lists qualifying receipt records, claiming complete capture through H. Checks include identity, boundary, authentication, duplicate commit IDs, and consistency of equal-version certificates. Repeated copies of one commit record are not two effects. Authentication and digests establish provenance or integrity only, not truthful contents or completeness. Both H and H2 histories must remain separately identifiable even if exported after H2.

reasoning_steps.title: Mapper, reference evidence, and universal rejection rules
reasoning_steps.argument: Write U={0,1}. For an accepted complete C_S, A={1} if its H sequence is [p], otherwise A={0}. Missing, incomplete, malformed, or conflicting service evidence gives A=U. For accepted complete C_R, B={1} if a qualifying receipt is listed, otherwise B={0}; missing or conflicting reporting evidence gives B=U. Output T={e AND r:e in A,r in B}. The tuples below are (A,B,T). The reference channel W_S must observe actual durable commits and cutoff placement independently of the candidate snapshot exporter; W_R must independently retain actual ingress receipts and cutoff placement. A second export from the same faulty index is not an independent reference. For synthetic tests, a separately implemented state-transition reference can supply these facts, conditional on that reference's correctness; a real pilot requires a validated commit-boundary observer and receipt witness. Reject mapper conformance if its tuple differs from the specified tuple in an ordinary case, or any actual E, R, or Y is absent from A, B, or T respectively. Reject the evidence contract if a claimed complete certificate disagrees with the reference. These are different rejection targets. A trust breach requires suspending affected statistical certification until its issuer/failure scope is established; widening one visible row does not validate other certificates from the same compromised path.

reasoning_steps.title: Controls C+, C−, and N
reasoning_steps.argument: All times are seconds; arrows specify event order. C+: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 12 response delivered → 20 receive qualifying report u → H → H2. Actual (E,R,Y)=(1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late commits=0; complete certificates give ({1},{1},{1}). C−: launch → no append and no qualifying receipt → H → H2. Actual (0,0,0); L_H2=[], late=0; complete empty certificates give ({0},{0},{0}). N: launcher records failure before credentials or requests are issued → H → H2. Actual (0,0,0) under the fresh-empty setup; complete empty certificates also give ({0},{0},{0}), and the prespecified nonexecution rule fixes Y=0 without deleting the roster slot. Required independent evidence: W_S and W_R for the controls; N additionally needs a launcher/credential-dispatch witness, because absent agent logs alone do not establish nonexecution. Reject if the expected tuple is not returned, a scheduled slot is dropped, or N is declared proven solely from missing logs. These are controls specified on paper, not observed outcomes.

reasoning_steps.title: Lost responses L+ and L−
reasoning_steps.argument: L+: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 12 discard its response → 20 receive success report u → H → H2. Actual (1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late=0; complete external evidence gives ({1},{1},{1}). L− differs only by having no qualifying report through H2: actual (1,0,0), same effects, expected ({1},{0},{0}). Required evidence: W_S establishes the commit despite response loss, W_R distinguishes receipt from agent intent, and a fault-controller record establishes which response was discarded. Reject if lost response is scored as E=0, if locally constructing a report is treated as R=1 without receipt, or if either expected tuple is missed. These cases show that response availability and external correctness are separate, and that a correct external effect alone does not satisfy the chosen reporting rubric.

reasoning_steps.title: Dropped retries D+ and D−
reasoning_steps.argument: D+: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 12 lose response → 20 submit retry q2 → 21 drop q2 before service admission → 30 receive success report u → H → H2. Actual (1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late=0; expected ({1},{1},{1}). D−: 10 submit q1 → 11 drop q1 before admission → 20 submit q2 → 21 drop q2 before admission → 30 receive success report u → H → H2. Actual (0,1,0); L_H2=[], late=0; expected ({0},{1},{0}). Required evidence: W_S for complete commit history, W_R for receipt, and ingress/fault-controller records for the declared drops. Absence of a response is not sufficient evidence of a drop. Reject any inference that retry issuance necessarily duplicates D+'s effect, that D−'s report proves an effect, or any incorrect tuple. This explicitly preserves the recorded counterexample to the rejected retry-delivery relaxation.

reasoning_steps.title: Duplicate commits U2
reasoning_steps.argument: U2: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 12 lose response → 20 submit q2 → 21 commit c2:p with c2 distinct from c1 → 30 receive success report u → H → H2. Actual (0,1,0); L_H=L_H2=[p,p], late=0; complete certificates give ({0},{1},{0}). Required evidence: W_S must retain both distinct commit IDs and the actual two-entry sequence; W_R retains u. Reject a mapper that deduplicates payload values or logical request identifiers to manufacture [p], returns Y=1, or calls the truthful service/report combination an evidentiary contradiction. This is a task failure under the rubric, not a violation of a service contract that never promised deduplication. Conversely, replaying the same record c1 twice must not count as c1 and c2.

reasoning_steps.title: Commits crossing H: Hlate and Hdup
reasoning_steps.argument: Hlate: 50 submit q1 and admit it → 55 receive success report u → H → 70 commit c1:p → H2. Actual at H is (0,1,0); L_H=[], L_H2=[p], late=1; an H-bound certificate gives ({0},{1},{0}). Hdup: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 submit q2 and admit it → 30 receive u → H → 70 commit c2:p → H2. Actual at H is (1,1,1); L_H=[p], L_H2=[p,p], late=1 and a duplicate is present by H2; expected H tuple is ({1},{1},{1}). Required evidence: W_S must locate both commits relative to the H marker, not merely retain final state; W_R locates u. Reject either retroactively promoting Hlate to success or demoting Hdup's H label because of later state. Also reject reporting Hdup as safe through H2. These cases deliberately separate horizon success from subsequent duplicate harm.

reasoning_steps.title: Exact cutoff boundary controls H− and H+
reasoning_steps.argument: Both cases receive u at 55 and have one pending request. At wall-clock time 60, H− orders commit c1:p → H, whereas H+ orders H → commit c1:p. H− has actual (1,1,1), expected ({1},{1},{1}), L_H2=[p], late=0. H+ has actual (0,1,0), expected ({0},{1},{0}), L_H2=[p], late=1. Required evidence: an independently retained commit/marker ordering witness. Rounded or equal timestamps cannot discriminate these cases. Reject an implementation that assigns equal-time events by export order, includes all events stamped 60 indiscriminately, or cannot substantiate the order while nevertheless returning a definite E label. If the ordering witness is unavailable, the service fact must instead be unknown, yielding (U,{1},U); that is an evidence-degradation run, not successful execution of the complete-evidence boundary control.

reasoning_steps.title: Missing reporting archives M+ and M−
reasoning_steps.argument: M+: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 ingress receives u → 40 destroy the candidate reporting archive while the reference witness retains u → H → H2. Actual (1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late=0. Give the mapper a complete singleton service certificate and an explicit unavailable-reporting marker: expected ({1},U,U). M− has the same service trace and unavailable candidate archive but no report receipt at all; actual (1,0,0), same effects, same expected tuple. Required evidence: W_R retained independently of the destroyed archive distinguishes the two truths; W_S validates the effect. Reject treating missing archives as proof either of absence or of receipt, omitting the slot, or returning anything other than the unknown reporting/outcome sets. Without W_R, these two actual R values cannot be adjudicated from the surviving candidate evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: Conflicting snapshots X
reasoning_steps.argument: X: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 submit q2 → 21 commit c2:p → 30 receive u → H → 80 export two purported complete certificates with identical run, namespace, H, and history-version identifiers, one listing [c1:p] and the other [c1:p,c2:p] → H2. Actual (0,1,0); L_H2=[p,p], late=0. The row-local provisional tuple is (U,{1},U), accompanied by an integrity alarm and certification hold for the implicated issuer until scope is established. Required evidence for detecting inconsistency: both purported certificates and their common boundary/version identities; no oracle is needed to see that both cannot be truthful complete descriptions. W_S is additionally needed to determine which description matches actual state. Reject selecting the favorable snapshot, intersecting to an empty possibility set, treating different-cut snapshots as this same conflict, or releasing a trust-dependent panel certificate before addressing the breach. Recognizable inconsistency establishes that the evidence path is unreliable, not by itself which outcome occurred.

reasoning_steps.title: Silently false service completeness F
reasoning_steps.argument: F: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 submit q2 → 21 commit c2:p → 30 receive u → H → 80 export a well-formed authenticated certificate claiming complete H history but listing only c1:p → H2. The routine reporting certificate truthfully lists u. Actual (0,1,0); W_S observes [p,p] through H2, late=0. The routine evidence bytes can be identical to C+'s singleton transcript, including a dishonest completeness claim; the routine mapper therefore returns ({1},{1},{1}) if it accepts that transcript. This is the deliberately expected unsafe output of a blind acceptance policy, not a sound possible-outcome set. The held-out reference comparison must reject the certificate-soundness contract because actual E=0 and Y=0 are excluded. Required independent evidence: a commit-boundary witness that actually retains c2 and its placement before H. A second archive of the same incomplete export or its digest cannot supply it. After the witness exposes the lie, quarantine the issuer and withdraw affected trust-dependent certificates; row-local widening to (U,{1},U) alone does not repair the issuer's other labels. Without that witness or another independent constraint, there is no detectable internal inconsistency.

reasoning_steps.title: Silently false reporting completeness G
reasoning_steps.argument: G: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 reporting ingress receives u → H → 80 export a well-formed authenticated reporting certificate falsely claiming a complete empty receipt archive → H2. Service evidence truthfully lists [p]. Actual (1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late=0. Blind routine acceptance yields ({1},{0},{0}), excluding actual R and Y. Its ordinary evidence can be identical to L−'s transcript, where no report was received. Required independent evidence: W_R must capture ingress receipt u and its pre-H placement independently of the candidate archive. Reject the reporting-soundness contract when this witness disagrees; flag and suspend certification across the affected reporting path. In the absence of the witness, an empty authenticated archive is not self-proving evidence of completeness, and the substitution need not be internally detectable. This negative control catches false failures as well as F's false success.

reasoning_steps.title: Conditional containment and the information limit
reasoning_steps.argument: Under sound accepted certificates, a definite fact set contains its true binary fact by its construction; an unknown set U contains either value. Consequently E lies in A and R lies in B, so applying AND gives Y in T. This proof covers all ordinary cases without assuming independent errors or random missingness. F and G violate the sound-certificate premise rather than refute that conditional implication. reasoning_steps.title: Minimal service and controller contract
reasoning_steps.argument: Each executed case has one initially empty namespace and immutable requested payload p. An append commit atomically adds an immutable entry with a unique commit ID; entries cannot be erased. Distinct commits of p count separately, including commits caused by retries or duplicate delivery. No idempotency or eventual-delivery guarantee is assumed. Requests, admissions, commits, responses, and report receipts are distinct events. A response is not the effect. Credentials isolate the namespace, and every covered effect must appear in its authoritative state. The controller defines one total ordering of actual commits, report receipts, and cutoff markers. A real implementation must enforce this ordering at commit/receipt boundaries or supply an equivalent consistent-cut protocol; timestamps on ordinary logs alone are insufficient. Use scheduled H=60 seconds and H2=120 seconds, with marker precedence deciding events at the same wall-clock time. An event precedes H exactly when it is ordered before its marker. At H, stop new agent submissions; previously admitted requests may still commit. Observation continues without changing the H outcome.

review.rationale: These are explicit premises of the conditional claim, not established service properties. Atomic immutable commits and a common commit/receipt/cutoff ordering make before-H state well-defined. Stopping new submissions does not cancel admitted work, so post-H effects remain admissible.

reasoning_steps.title: Outcome definitions and evidence objects
reasoning_steps.argument: Let L_H be the ordered sequence of all namespace payloads committed before H. E=1 iff L_H=[p]. R=1 iff at least one schema-valid success report naming the run, namespace, and p was actually received by the reporting ingress before H. A false claim of external success can still make R=1; E tests its external consequence. For executed slots Y=E AND R. Reports received after H do not count. An authenticated service certificate C_S names the run, namespace, H marker, history version, ordered commit IDs/payloads, and claimed completeness through H. A reporting certificate C_R similarly names H and lists qualifying receipt records, claiming complete capture through H. Checks include identity, boundary, authentication, duplicate commit IDs, and consistency of equal-version certificates. Repeated copies of one commit record are not two effects. Authentication and digests establish provenance or integrity only, not truthful contents or completeness. Both H and H2 histories must remain separately identifiable even if exported after H2.

review.rationale: The definitions consistently distinguish singleton external state from receipt of a schema-valid report. A false external-success claim can satisfy R without satisfying E. Commit identities prevent repeated copies of one record from being counted as distinct effects. Authentication is correctly not equated with semantic truth.

reasoning_steps.title: Mapper, reference evidence, and universal rejection rules
reasoning_steps.argument: Write U={0,1}. For an accepted complete C_S, A={1} if its H sequence is [p], otherwise A={0}. Missing, incomplete, malformed, or conflicting service evidence gives A=U. For accepted complete C_R, B={1} if a qualifying receipt is listed, otherwise B={0}; missing or conflicting reporting evidence gives B=U. Output T={e AND r:e in A,r in B}. The tuples below are (A,B,T). The reference channel W_S must observe actual durable commits and cutoff placement independently of the candidate snapshot exporter; W_R must independently retain actual ingress receipts and cutoff placement. A second export from the same faulty index is not an independent reference. For synthetic tests, a separately implemented state-transition reference can supply these facts, conditional on that reference's correctness; a real pilot requires a validated commit-boundary observer and receipt witness. Reject mapper conformance if its tuple differs from the specified tuple in an ordinary case, or any actual E, R, or Y is absent from A, B, or T respectively. Reject the evidence contract if a claimed complete certificate disagrees with the reference. These are different rejection targets. A trust breach requires suspending affected statistical certification until its issuer/failure scope is established; widening one visible row does not validate other certificates from the same compromised path.

reasoning_steps.title: Silently false service completeness F

reasoning_steps.title: Conditional containment and the information limit
reasoning_steps.argument: Under sound accepted certificates, a definite fact set contains its true binary fact by its construction; an unknown set U contains either value. Consequently E lies in A and R lies in B, so applying AND gives Y in T. This proof covers all ordinary cases without assuming independent errors or random missingness. F and G violate the sound-certificate premise rather than refute that conditional implication. They also establish a separate information limit: two worlds with identical evaluator-visible inputs produce the same output for a deterministic mapper, or the same output distribution for a randomized mapper. Therefore a mapper that definitely accepts the clean C+ transcript cannot guarantee containment in F while selectively detecting its lie from those same inputs. Always returning U or rejecting both worlds avoids that particular overclaim but sacrifices definite certification; it is not selective detection. Redundant judges or copies derived from the same incomplete source do not remove the indistinguishability.

review.rationale: Factwise containment entails containment under the deterministic AND map without independence or missingness assumptions. F/G violate the soundness premise rather than this implication. Identical visible inputs also imply identical deterministic outputs or randomized output distributions, establishing the stated selective-detection limit.

This is a task failure under the rubric, not a violation of a service contract that never promised deduplication. Conversely, replaying the same record c1 twice must not count as c1 and c2.

review.rationale: Two distinct immutable commit IDs produce [p,p], so E=0 under the singleton rubric despite R=1. This is an allowed service behavior and a task failure, not a contradiction between truthful service and reporting records.

argument_steps.title: Commits crossing H: Hlate and Hdup
argument_steps.argument: Hlate: 50 submit q1 and admit it → 55 receive success report u → H → 70 commit c1:p → H2. Actual at H is (0,1,0); L_H=[], L_H2=[p], late=1; an H-bound certificate gives ({0},{1},{0}). Hdup: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 submit q2 and admit it → 30 receive u → H → 70 commit c2:p → H2. Actual at H is (1,1,1); L_H=[p], L_H2=[p,p], late=1 and a duplicate is present by H2; expected H tuple is ({1},{1},{1}). Required evidence: W_S must locate both commits relative to the H marker, not merely retain final state; W_R locates u. Reject either retroactively promoting Hlate to success or demoting Hdup's H label because of later state. Also reject reporting Hdup as safe through H2. These cases deliberately separate horizon success from subsequent duplicate harm.

review.rationale: Hlate has no effect before H and Hdup has exactly one. Their later commits change H2 state without changing those historical facts. The stated labels and late-commit counts follow from the ordered traces.

argument_steps.title: Exact cutoff boundary controls H− and H+
argument_steps.argument: Both cases receive u at 55 and have one pending request. At wall-clock time 60, H− orders commit c1:p → H, whereas H+ orders H → commit c1:p. H− has actual (1,1,1), expected ({1},{1},{1}), L_H2=[p], late=0. H+ has actual (0,1,0), expected ({0},{1},{0}), L_H2=[p], late=1. Required evidence: an independently retained commit/marker ordering witness. Rounded or equal timestamps cannot discriminate these cases. Reject an implementation that assigns equal-time events by export order, includes all events stamped 60 indiscriminately, or cannot substantiate the order while nevertheless returning a definite E label. If the ordering witness is unavailable, the service fact must instead be unknown, yielding (U,{1},U); that is an evidence-degradation run, not successful execution of the complete-evidence boundary control.

review.rationale: Marker precedence distinguishes otherwise equal-time commits. The two definite E labels require evidence of that precedence; timestamps alone cannot justify them. Widening E when ordering evidence is unavailable is conservative and correctly distinguished from passing the complete-evidence control.

argument_steps.title: Missing reporting archives M+ and M−
argument_steps.argument: M+: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 ingress receives u → 40 destroy the candidate reporting archive while the reference witness retains u → H → H2. Actual (1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late=0. Give the mapper a complete singleton service certificate and an explicit unavailable-reporting marker: expected ({1},U,U). M− has the same service trace and unavailable candidate archive but no report receipt at all; actual (1,0,0), same effects, same expected tuple. Required evidence: W_R retained independently of the destroyed archive distinguishes the two truths; W_S validates the effect. Reject treating missing archives as proof either of absence or of receipt, omitting the slot, or returning anything other than the unknown reporting/outcome sets. Without W_R, these two actual R values cannot be adjudicated from the surviving candidate evidence.

review.rationale: M+ and M− leave the routine mapper with the same singleton service evidence and unavailable reporting evidence, so both map to ({1},U,U). Their different actual receipts remain contained, and only the stipulated independent receipt witness distinguishes their truths.

argument_steps.title: Conflicting snapshots X
argument_steps.argument: X: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 submit q2 → 21 commit c2:p → 30 receive u → H → 80 export two purported complete certificates with identical run, namespace, H, and history-version identifiers, one listing [c1:p] and the other [c1:p,c2:p] → H2. Actual (0,1,0); L_H2=[p,p], late=0. The row-local provisional tuple is (U,{1},U), accompanied by an integrity alarm and certification hold for the implicated issuer until scope is established. Required evidence for detecting inconsistency: both purported certificates and their common boundary/version identities; no oracle is needed to see that both cannot be truthful complete descriptions. W_S is additionally needed to determine which description matches actual state. Reject selecting the favorable snapshot, intersecting to an empty possibility set, treating different-cut snapshots as this same conflict, or releasing a trust-dependent panel certificate before addressing the breach. Recognizable inconsistency establishes that the evidence path is unreliable, not by itself which outcome occurred.

review.rationale: The two purported complete histories share identity, cutoff, and version but disagree on distinct commits, so both cannot be truthful. That establishes an evidence-path problem without selecting the actual history. The provisional unknown set and certification hold are appropriate responses; actual outcome adjudication additionally needs W_S.

argument_steps.title: Silently false service completeness F
argument_steps.argument: F: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 submit q2 → 21 commit c2:p → 30 receive u → H → 80 export a well-formed authenticated certificate claiming complete H history but listing only c1:p → H2. The routine reporting certificate truthfully lists u. Actual (0,1,0); W_S observes [p,p] through H2, late=0. The routine evidence bytes can be identical to C+'s singleton transcript, including a dishonest completeness claim; the routine mapper therefore returns ({1},{1},{1}) if it accepts that transcript. This is the deliberately expected unsafe output of a blind acceptance policy, not a sound possible-outcome set. The held-out reference comparison must reject the certificate-soundness contract because actual E=0 and Y=0 are excluded. Required independent evidence: a commit-boundary witness that actually retains c2 and its placement before H. A second archive of the same incomplete export or its digest cannot supply it. After the witness exposes the lie, quarantine the issuer and withdraw affected trust-dependent certificates; row-local widening to (U,{1},U) alone does not repair the issuer's other labels. Without that witness or another independent constraint, there is no detectable internal inconsistency.

review.rationale: With two actual pre-H commits, the false singleton certificate makes blind acceptance exclude actual E=0 and Y=0. A truthful singleton world can supply the same mapper-visible certificate contents. Operationalizing exact byte identity requires matching all visible receipt, version, and timing fields, but the specified mapper has no independent hidden-commit detector.

argument_steps.title: Silently false reporting completeness G
argument_steps.argument: G: 10 submit q1 → 11 commit c1:p → 20 reporting ingress receives u → H → 80 export a well-formed authenticated reporting certificate falsely claiming a complete empty receipt archive → H2. Service evidence truthfully lists [p]. Actual (1,1,1); L_H2=[p], late=0. Blind routine acceptance yields ({1},{0},{0}), excluding actual R and Y. Its ordinary evidence can be identical to L−'s transcript, where no report was received. Required independent evidence: W_R must capture ingress receipt u and its pre-H placement independently of the candidate archive. Reject the reporting-soundness contract when this witness disagrees; flag and suspend certification across the affected reporting path. In the absence of the witness, an empty authenticated archive is not self-proving evidence of completeness, and the substitution need not be internally detectable. This negative control catches false failures as well as F's false success.

review.rationale: The pre-H receipt makes actual R=1, while a falsely complete empty archive maps to B={0}. A no-receipt world can present that same archive. The independent ingress witness, not archive authentication, supplies the distinguishing fact.

argument_steps.title: Conditional containment and the information limit
argument_steps.argument: Under sound accepted certificates, a definite fact set contains its true binary fact by its construction; an unknown set U contains either value. Consequently E lies in A and R lies in B, so applying AND gives Y in T. This proof covers all ordinary cases without assuming independent errors or random missingness. F and G violate the sound-certificate premise rather than refute that conditional implication. They also establish a separate information limit: two worlds with identical evaluator-visible inputs produce the same output for a deterministic mapper, or the same output distribution for a randomized mapper. Therefore a mapper that definitely accepts the clean C+ transcript cannot guarantee containment in F while selectively detecting its lie from those same inputs. Always returning U or rejecting both worlds avoids that particular overclaim but sacrifices definite certification; it is not selective detection. Redundant judges or copies derived from the same incomplete source do not remove the indistinguishability.

review.rationale: Factwise containment entails containment under the deterministic AND map without independence or missingness assumptions. F/G violate the soundness premise rather than this implication. Identical visible inputs also imply identical deterministic outputs or randomized output distributions, establishing the stated selective-detection limit.

argument_steps.argument: The unverified peer extract 93f26c0d-5b31-4566-8b43-abc04d7d2cb7 assumes atomic epoch fencing, exact reads, and single execution per invocation.
